arXiv:1008.4248v1 [math.NA] 25 Aug 2010

NOTES ON ERROR ESTIMATES FOR GALERKIN APPROXIMATIONS OF THE ‘CLASSICAL’ BOUSSINESQ SYSTEM AND RELATED HYPERBOLIC PROBLEMS.

D.C. Antonopoulos Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Athens, 15784 Zographou, Greece Email address: antonod@math.uoa.gr and V.A. Dougalis Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Athens, 15784 Zographou, Greece, and Institute of Applied and Computational Mathematics, FORTH, 70013 Heraklion, Greece Email address: doug@math.uoa.gr
Abstract.

We consider the ‘classical’ Boussinesq system in one space dimension and its symmetric analog. These systems model two-way propagation of nonlinear, dispersive long waves of small amplitude on the surface of an ideal fluid in a uniform horizontal channel. We discretize an initial-boundary-value problem for these systems in space using Galerkin-finite element methods and prove error estimates for the resulting semidiscrete problems and also for their fully discrete analogs effected by explicit Runge-Kutta time-stepping procedures. The theoretical orders of convergence obtained are consistent with the results of numerical experiments that are also presented.

Key words and phrases: 
Boussinesq systems, nonlinear dispersive waves, first-order hyperbolics, Galerkin methods, error estimates
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
65M60, 35Q53;

1. Introduction

In this paper we will analyze Galerkin approximations to the so-called ‘classical’ Boussinesq system

ηt\displaystyle\eta_{t} +ux+(η​u)x=0,\displaystyle+u_{x}+(\eta u)_{x}=0\,, (1.1)
ut\displaystyle u_{t} +ηx+u​ux−13​ux​x​t=0,\displaystyle+\eta_{x}+uu_{x}-\tfrac{1}{3}u_{xxt}=0\,,

which is an approximation of the two-dimensional Euler equations of water-wave theory that models two-way propagation of long waves of small amplitude on the surface of an ideal fluid in a uniform horizontal channel of finite depth. The variables in (1.1)(\ref{eq11}) are nondimensional and unscaled; xx and tt are proportional to position along the channel and time, respectively, and η=η⁡(x,t)\eta=\eta(x,t) and u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) are proportional to the elevation of the free surface above a level of rest represented by η=0\eta=0, and to the depth-averaged mean horizontal velocity of the fluid.

The system (1.1)(\ref{eq11}) is a member of a general family of Boussinesq systems derived in [11] that are approximations to the Euler equations of the same order as (1.1)(\ref{eq11}) and whose nonlinear and dispersive terms are of equal importance when written in scaled form. These systems are written as

ηt\displaystyle\eta_{t} +ux+(η​u)x+a​ux​x​x−b​ηx​x​t=0,\displaystyle+u_{x}+(\eta u)_{x}+au_{xxx}-b\eta_{xxt}=0\,, (1.2)
ut\displaystyle u_{t} +ηx+u​ux+c​ηx​x​x−d​ux​x​t=0,\displaystyle+\eta_{x}+uu_{x}+c\eta_{xxx}-du_{xxt}=0\,,

where aa, bb, cc, dd are real parameters satisfying a+b=12​(θ2−1/3)a+b=\tfrac{1}{2}(\theta^{2}-1/3), c+d=12​(1−θ2)c+d=\tfrac{1}{2}(1-\theta^{2}), where 0≤θ≤10\leq\theta\leq 1. The specific system (1.1)(\ref{eq11}) has been previously formally derived from the Euler equations, in the appropriate parameter regime, in [24], [26], and [31]. It has been widely used in the engineering fluid mechanics literature for computations of long, nonlinear dispersive waves, starting with [24] and [25].

Existence and uniqueness of the initial-value problem for (1.1)(\ref{eq11}) posed for x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and t≥0t\geq 0 and supplemented by initial conditions of the form

η⁡(x,0)=η0​(x),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),x∈ℝ,\eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\,,\quad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\,,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}\,, (1.3)

was studied by Schonbeck, [27] and Amick, [2]. In these papers global existence and uniqueness was established for infinitely differentiable initial data of compact support such that η0​(x)>−1\eta_{0}(x)>-1, x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. In [12] the theory of [27] and [2] was used to prove that given initial data (η0,u0)∈Hs​(ℝ)×Hs+1​(ℝ)(\eta_{0},u_{0})\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s+1}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥1s\geq 1, such that infx∈ℝη0​(x)>−1\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\eta_{0}(x)>-1, there is a unique solution (η,u)(\eta,u) which, for any T>0T>0, lies in C⁡(0,T,Hs​(ℝ))×C⁡(0,T,Hs+1​(ℝ))C(0,T;H^{s}(\mathbb{R}))\times C(0,T;H^{s+1}(\mathbb{R})). (Here, Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) is the usual, L2L^{2}-based Sobolev space of functions on ℝ\mathbb{R} and C⁡(0,T,X)C(0,T;X) denotes the space of functions ϕ=ϕ⁡(t)\phi=\phi(t) having, for each t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], values in a Banach space XX and are such that the map [0,T]↦‖ϕ‖X[0,T]\mapsto\|\phi\|_{X} is continuous.)

It is well known that the initial-value problem (1.1)(\ref{eq11}), (1.3)(\ref{eq13}) has classical solitary-wave solutions. In [4] we review the properties of such solutions, we construct them numerically and investigate, by means of numerical experiments, the resolution of general initial profiles into sequences of solitary waves, the details of the interaction of solitary waves during head-on and overtaking collisions, the interaction of solitary waves with boundaries, and several other issues. These numerical experiments were performed in [4] by fully discrete Galerkin methods that approximate solutions of (1.1)(\ref{eq11}) posed on finite intervals and subject to boundary conditions. It is of interest therefore to study initial-boundary-value problems for (1.1)(\ref{eq11}) and establish error estimates for their numerical approximations.

In this paper we shall analyze the numerical solution of the following initial-boundary-value problem (ibvp) for (1.1)(\ref{eq11}): For some 0<T<∞0<T<\infty, we seek η=η⁡(x,t)\eta=\eta(x,t), u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t), defined for 0≤x≤10\leq x\leq 1, 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T, and satisfying

ηt\displaystyle\eta_{t} +ux+(ηu)x=0,(x,t)∈[0,1]×[0,T],\displaystyle+u_{x}+(\eta u)_{x}=0\,,\qquad\qquad(x,t)\in[0,1]\times[0,T]\,, (CB)
ut\displaystyle u_{t} +ηx+uux−13ux​x​t=0,(x,t)∈[0,1]×[0,T],\displaystyle+\eta_{x}+uu_{x}-\tfrac{1}{3}u_{xxt}=0\,,\quad(x,t)\in[0,1]\times[0,T]\,,
η⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\eta( x,0)=η0(x),u(x,0)=u0(x),x∈[0,1],\displaystyle x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\,,\quad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\,,\quad x\in[0,1]\,,
u⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle u( 0,t)=0,u(1,t)=0,t∈[0,T].\displaystyle 0,t)=0\,,\quad u(1,t)=0\,,\quad t\in[0,T]\,.

This ibvp (for 0<t<∞0<t<\infty) has been studied by Adamy, [1], who showed that it has weak (distributional) solutions (η,u)∈L∞​(ℝ+,L1×H01)(\eta,u)\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{+};L^{1}\times H_{0}^{1}) provided e.g. that η0∈L1\eta_{0}\in L^{1}, u0∈H01u_{0}\in H_{0}^{1} with infx∈[0,1]η0​(x)>−1\inf_{x\in[0,1]}\eta_{0}(x)>-1. (Here L1=L1​(0,1)L^{1}=L^{1}(0,1), and H01=H01​(0,1)H_{0}^{1}=H_{0}^{1}(0,1) is the subspace of the Sobolev space H1​(0,1)H^{1}(0,1) whose elements vanish at x=0x=0 and x=1x=1.) The proof uses a parabolic regularization of the first pde of (CB)(\ref{cb}), a technique used in the context of the Cauchy problem by Schonbeck, [27]. It should be noted that the homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on uu in (CB)(\ref{cb}) are one kind of boundary conditions that lead to well posed ibvp’s in the case of the linearized system, [21]. It is noteworthy that the CB system needs only two boundary conditions for well-posedness as opposed to the four boundary conditions (for example, Dirichlet conditions on η\eta and uu at each endpoint of the interval) required in the case of other Boussinesq systems, such as the BBM-BBM (a=c=0a=c=0, b=db=d in (1.2)(\ref{eq12}),[10]), or the Bona-Smith systems (a=0a=0, b=d>0b=d>0, c<0c<0 in (1.2)(\ref{eq12}), [7].) The case of the homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions in (CB)(\ref{cb}) may be viewed as a base for studying the nonhomogeneous analog wherein u⁡(0,t)u(0,t) and u⁡(1,t)u(1,t) are given functions of t≥0t\geq 0 corresponding to measurements of the velocity variable at two points along the channel.

In [13], Bona, Colin, and Lannes introduced another type of Boussinesq systems that they called ‘completely symmetric’. These are obtained by a nonlinear change of variables from the usual systems (1.2)(\ref{eq12}), and have certain mathematical and modelling advantages over the latter. In this paper we shall also therefore consider the analogous problem for the symmetric system, specifically the ibvp

ηt\displaystyle\qquad\eta_{t} +ux+12(ηu)x=0,(x,t)∈[0,1]×[0,T],\displaystyle+u_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}(\eta u)_{x}=0\,,\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad(x,t)\in[0,1]\times[0,T]\,, (SCB)
ut\displaystyle u_{t} +ηx+32uux+12ηηx−13ux​x​t=0,(x,t)∈[0,1]×[0,T],\displaystyle+\eta_{x}+\tfrac{3}{2}uu_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}\eta\eta_{x}-\tfrac{1}{3}u_{xxt}=0\,,\quad(x,t)\in[0,1]\times[0,T]\,,
η⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\eta( x,0)=η0(x),u(x,0)=u0(x),x∈[0,1],\displaystyle x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\,,\quad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\,,\quad x\in[0,1]\,,
u⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle u( 0,t)=0,u(1,t)=0,t∈[0,T].\displaystyle 0,t)=0\,,\quad u(1,t)=0\,,\quad t\in[0,T]\,.

It is not hard to see that the solution of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) satisfies the conservation property

‖η⁡(t)‖2+‖u⁡(t)‖2+13​‖ux​(t)‖2=‖η0‖2+‖u0‖2+13​‖u0′‖2,\|\eta(t)\|^{2}+\|u(t)\|^{2}+\tfrac{1}{3}\|u_{x}(t)\|^{2}=\|\eta_{0}\|^{2}+\|u_{0}\|^{2}+\tfrac{1}{3}\|u_{0}^{\prime}\|^{2}\,, (1.4)

for t≥0t\geq 0, which simplifies the study of its well-posedness and the analysis of its numerical approximations as will be seen in the sequel.

In this paper we shall analyze semidiscrete and fully discrete Galerkin-finite element methods for the ibvp’s (CB)(\ref{cb}) and (SCB)(\ref{scb}) assuming that their solutions are sufficiently smooth. Previously, rigorous error estimates for Galerkin methods for these ‘classical’ Boussinesq systems were proved in the case of the periodic initial-value problem in [3] and [9]. (For numerical work for this type and for other Boussinesq systems of the form (1.2)(\ref{eq12}) we refer the reader e.g. to [3], [6], [5], [22], [23], [10], [8], [14], [15], [18], [4].)

The analysis of Galerkin methods for (CB)(\ref{cb}) or (SCB)(\ref{scb}) is of considerable interest due to the loss of optimal order of accuracy that emerges from the error estimates and is also supported by the numerical experiments. We shall investigate this phenomenon in detail in the paper but one may in general say that in the uniform spatial mesh case the (limited) loss of accuracy seems to be due to a combination of effects related to the boundary conditions and the specific form of the ‘classical’ Boussinesq systems. (For example, no loss of accuracy occurs in the case of periodic boundary conditions on η\eta and uu for these systems, cf. [3], [9].) In the case of general (quasiuniform) mesh the (more severe) loss of accuracy seems to stem from the lack of cancellation effects that are present in the uniform mesh case, and from the hyperbolic character of the first p.d.e. of these systems. (The loss of optimal order of accuracy in standard Galerkin semidiscretizations of first-order hyperbolic equations manifested in various contexts is well known and was early observed e.g. by Dupont in [20].)

In section 22 we consider the standard Galerkin semidiscretizations of (CB)(\ref{cb}) and (SCB)(\ref{scb}) in the space of piecewise linear, continuous functions. In the case of a quasiuniform mesh, we prove that if the solution (η,u)(\eta,u) of (CB)(\ref{cb}) or (SCB)(\ref{scb}) is sufficiently smooth and (ηh,uh)(\eta_{h},u_{h}) is the semidiscrete approximation, then ‖η−ηh‖=O⁡(h)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|=O(h) and ‖u−uh‖1=O⁡(h)\|u-u_{h}\|_{1}=O(h). (Here ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|, ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} denote, respectively, the L2L^{2} and H1H^{1} norms on [0,1][0,1].) In the case of uniform mesh, a suitable superaccuracy result for the error of the interpolant into the finite element subspace (a consequence of cancellations due to the uniform mesh) affords proving the improved estimates ‖η−ηh‖=O⁡(h3/2)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|=O(h^{3/2}) and ‖u−uh‖=O⁡(h2)\|u-u_{h}\|=O(h^{2}). These rates of convergence are confirmed by the numerical experiments at the end of the section.

In section 33 we turn to the semidiscretization of (CB)(\ref{cb}) or (SCB)(\ref{scb}) using as finite element subspace the C2C^{2} cubic splines. In the case of quasiuniform mesh we now get, as expected, ‖η−ηh‖=O⁡(h3)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|=O(h^{3}), ‖u−uh‖1=O⁡(h3)\|u-u_{h}\|_{1}=O(h^{3}), following the technique of the analogous proof in the previous section. Use of a uniform mesh and of relevant superconvergence results of Wahlbin, [30], allows proving a series of suitable superaccuracy estimates for the error of the interpolant and the error of the elliptic projection into the cubic spline subspaces. These results lead to error estimates such as ‖η−ηh‖=O⁡(h3.5​ln⁡1/h)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|=O(h^{3.5}\sqrt{\ln 1/h}), ‖u−uh‖=O⁡(h4​ln⁡1/h)\|u-u_{h}\|=O(h^{4}\sqrt{\ln 1/h}), that are consistent with the rates of convergence of the errors obtained from numerical experiments.

In section 44 we turn to the analysis of fully discrete schemes. We consider only explicit time-stepping schemes in order to avoid the more costly implicit methods that require solving nonlinear systems of equations at every time step. Of course, with explicit methods there arises the issue of stability of the fully discrete schemes. We confine ourselves to a uniform mesh spatial discretization and consider three representative explicit Runge-Kutta schemes, namely, the Euler, the improved Euler, and the classical, four-stage, Runge-Kutta methods, whose orders of accuracy are 11, 22, and 44, respectively. We couple the Euler and improved Euler schemes with a piecewise linear spatial discretization and the fourth-order RK scheme with cubic splines. We show that the stability restrictions on the time step kk needed by these schemes are of form k=O⁡(h2)k=O(h^{2}), k=O⁡(h4/3)k=O(h^{4/3}), and k≤λ0​hk\leq\lambda_{0}h for a constant λ0\lambda_{0} sufficiently small, for the schemes with Euler, improved Euler, and fourth-order RK temporal discretizations, respectively. Under these restrictions, we prove optimal-order in time error estimates for the fully discrete schemes; the spatial rates of convergence are these of the semidiscrete approximations. The evidence of numerical experiments is consistent with the theoretical results.

In section 55 we analyze a nonstandard Galerkin semidiscrete approximation of (CB)(\ref{cb}) and (SCB)(\ref{scb}) that approximates η\eta by piecewise linear continuous functions and uu by piecewise quadratic C1C^{1} functions defined on the same (uniform) mesh. (The method may be generalized using the analogous pairs of higher-order splines but here we confine ourselves to the low-order case.) A series of superaccuracy results for the error of the L2L^{2} projection onto the space of piecewise linear continuous functions is developed, one of which makes use of a result of Demko, [17], on the exponential decay of the off-diagonal elements of the inverse of a certain tridiagonal matrix. With the aid of these results we show optimal-order error estimates e.g. of the type ‖η−ηh‖=O⁡(h2)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|=O(h^{2}), ‖u−uh‖=O⁡(h3)\|u-u_{h}\|=O(h^{3}). Finally, in section 66 we make some remarks on the application of standard Galerkin methods on some simple first-order hyperbolic problems. Specifically, superaccuracy tools that were developed in the case of uniform mesh in previous sections are combined with further similar estimates proved in this section to provide the basis for extending the optimal-order L2L^{2} error estimate of Dupont, [20], for the periodic initial value problem, to the case of two types of initial-boundary value problems for first-order hyperbolics. The situation is contrasted with what happens in the case of nonuniform meshes by means of numerical examples.

2. Standard Galerkin semidiscretization with piecewise linear, continuous functions

2.1. Semidiscretization on a quasiuniform mesh

Upon choice of a basis for Sh2S_{h}^{2}, it is seen that the semidiscrete problems (2.7)(\ref{eq27})-(2.8)(\ref{eq28}) and (2.9)(\ref{eq29})-(2.10)(\ref{eq210}) represent initial-value problems for systems of o.d.e’s. Clearly, these systems have unique solutions at least locally in time. One conclusion of the next proposition is that they possess unique solutions up to t=Tt=T, where [0,T][0,T] will denote henceforth the interval of existence of solutions of (CB)(\ref{cb}) or (SCB)(\ref{scb}).

Proposition 2.1.

Let hh be sufficiently small. Remark 2.1.

It is not hard to see that the conclusions of Theorem 2.12.1 hold if we take ηh​(0)\eta_{h}(0) as any approximation of η0\eta_{0} in Sh2S_{h}^{2} with optimal-order L2L^{2} rate of convergence. However, uh​(0)u_{h}(0) has to be taken as Ih,0​u0I_{h,0}u_{0} or Rh​u0R_{h}u_{0}.

Remark 2.2.

The superaccuracy estimate ‖ξ‖1=O⁡(h3/2)\|\xi\|_{1}=O(h^{3/2}) of (2.25)(\ref{eq225}) combined with (2.3)(\ref{eq23}) and Sobolev’s inequality yields the L∞L^{\infty} estimate ‖u−uh‖∞=O⁡(h3/2)\|u-u_{h}\|_{\infty}=O(h^{3/2}) for uu.

Remark 2.3.

In the case of a quasiuniform mesh with h=maxi⁡(xi+1−xi)h=\max_{i}(x_{i+1}-x_{i}), one may easily check that the analog of Lemma 2.12.1 still holds; however in the proof of Lemma 2.22.2 there is no cancellation anymore from adjacent intervals and the conclusion is just that ‖ψ‖≤C​h\|\psi\|\leq Ch. As a consequence, the techniques of the proof of Theorem 2.12.1 now yield that ‖η−ηh‖=O⁡(h)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|=O(h) and ‖u−uh‖1=O⁡(h)\|u-u_{h}\|_{1}=O(h), and, instead of the optimal-order estimates in (i​i)(ii), that ‖u−uh‖=O⁡(h3/2)\|u-u_{h}\|=O(h^{3/2}) and ‖ut−uh​t‖=O⁡(h3/2)\|u_{t}-u_{ht}\|=O(h^{3/2}). However, for the linearized problem

u⁡(0,t)=0,u⁡(1,t)\displaystyle u(0,t)=0\,,\,\,\quad u(1,t) =0,t∈[0,T],\displaystyle=0\,,\quad t\in[0,T]\,,
η⁡(x,0)=η0​(x),u⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\,,\quad u( x,0)=u0(x),x∈[0,1],\displaystyle x,0)=u_{0}(x)\,,\quad x\in[0,1]\,,

the last two estimates may be improved to yield optimal order, i.e. to give ‖u−uh‖=O⁡(h2)\|u-u_{h}\|=O(h^{2}), ‖ut−uh​t‖=O⁡(h2)\|u_{t}-u_{ht}\|=O(h^{2}). Our numerical experiments suggest that ‖u−uh‖=O⁡(h2)\|u-u_{h}\|=O(h^{2}) even in the nonlinear case, but we have not been able to prove this thusfar.

2.3. Numerical experiments

We first consider the case of approximations on a uniform mesh with h=1/Nh=1/N on [0,1][0,1]. Table 2.1 shows the errors and the associated rates of convergence,

in the L2L^{2}-, L∞L^{\infty}- and H1H^{1}-norms at T=1T=1, of the standard Galerkin approximation (using piecewise linear, continuous functions) to the (CB)(\ref{cb}) system with suitable right-hand so that its exact solution is given by η=exp⁡(2​t)​(cos⁡(π​x)+x+2)\eta=\exp(2t)(\cos(\pi x)+x+2), u=exp⁡(−x​t)​x​sin⁡(π​x)u=\exp(-xt)x\sin(\pi x). The system was integrated up to T=1T=1 with the classical, four-stage, fourth-order explicit Runge-Kutta method (see Section 44) using a time step k=h/10k=h/10. We checked that the temporal error of the discretization was very small compared to the spatial error, so that the errors and rates of convergence shown are essentially those of the semidiscrete problem (2.7)(\ref{eq27}), (2.20)(\ref{eq220}). The table suggests that the L2L^{2} rates of convergence of η\eta and uu approach 3/23/2 and 22, respectively, thus confirming the relevant estimates of Theorem 2.12.1. It also suggests that ‖u−uh‖1=O⁡(h)\|u-u_{h}\|_{1}=O(h) (confirming the result of Theorem 2.12.1), and ‖η−ηh‖1=O⁡(h1/2)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|_{1}=O(h^{1/2}), ‖η−ηh‖∞=O⁡(h)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|_{\infty}=O(h), ‖u−uh‖∞=O⁡(h2)\|u-u_{h}\|_{\infty}=O(h^{2}). Table 2.2 shows the analogous errors and rates in the case of a nonhomogeneous (SCB)(\ref{scb}) system with the same exact solution η=exp⁡(2​t)​(cos⁡(π​x)+x+2)\eta=\exp(2t)(\cos(\pi x)+x+2), u=exp⁡(−x​t)​x​sin⁡(π​x)u=\exp(-xt)x\sin(\pi x), integrated on a uniform spatial mesh up to T=1T=1 with the same time stepping procedure. The convergence rates are essentially the same. We shall also derive a superaccuracy estimate for P⁡[(w​e)′]P[(we)^{\prime}], where ee is the error of the elliptic projection of a function v∈C05v\in C_{0}^{5} and ww is a C1C^{1} weight. Proposition 3.2.

Suppose that v∈C05v\in C_{0}^{5} and let vh=Rh​vv_{h}=R_{h}v be its elliptic projection onto Sh,04S_{h,0}^{4}. Then the following hold:

  • (i)(i)

    |(v−vh)′​(xi)|≤C​h4​‖v‖W∞5provideddist​(xi,∂I)≥C1​h​ln⁡1h,|(v-v_{h})^{\prime}(x_{i})|\leq Ch^{4}\|v\|_{W_{\infty}^{5}}\quad\text{provided}\quad\text{dist}(x_{i},\partial I)\geq C_{1}h\ln\tfrac{1}{h}\,, (3.13)

    where C1C_{1} is a sufficiently large constant independent of hh.

  • (i​i)(ii)

    If xix_{i}, xi+1x_{i+1} are two adjacent nodes for which the second inequality in (3.13)(\ref{eq313}) holds and e⁡(x)=v⁡(x)−vh​(x)e(x)=v(x)-v_{h}(x), we have

    e⁡(xi+1)−e⁡(xi)=O⁡(h5)​‖v‖W∞5.e(x_{i+1})-e(x_{i})=O(h^{5})\|v\|_{W_{\infty}^{5}}\,. (3.14)
Proof.

(i)(i) The estimate (3.13)(\ref{eq313}) follows from Corollary 1.6.21.6.2 of [30] (which is strictly valid when the elliptic projection is defined by (v~h′,ϕ′)=(v′,ϕ′)(\tilde{v}_{h}^{\prime},\phi^{\prime})=(v^{\prime},\phi^{\prime}) ∀ϕ∈Sh,04\forall\phi\in S_{h,0}^{4}), combined with Theorem 1.3.11.3.1 of [30] that allows us to state the result for vh=Rh​vv_{h}=R_{h}v defined as in section 22 of the paper at hand.

(i​i)(ii) The cancellation property expressed by (3.14)(\ref{eq314}) is a consequence of the fact that e~​(x)=v⁡(x)−v~h​(x)\tilde{e}(x)=v(x)-\tilde{v}_{h}(x) may be represented in the form

e~​(x)=Qi​(x)+O⁡(h5)​‖w‖W∞5​(xi,xi+1),x∈[xi,xi+1],\tilde{e}(x)=Q_{i}(x)+O(h^{5})\|w\|_{W_{\infty}^{5}(x_{i},x_{i+1})}\,,\quad x\in[x_{i},x_{i+1}]\,,

The results of the Theorem also hold if we take as ηh​(0)\eta_{h}(0) any other approximation of η0\eta_{0} in Sh4S_{h}^{4} of optimal order of accuracy in L2L^{2}.

3.3. Numerical experiments

We considered the nonhomogeneous (SCB)(\ref{scb}) system and we discretized it on a uniform mesh with diminishing h=1/Nh=1/N on [0,1][0,1]

using cubic splines for the spatial discretization and fourth-order accurate explicit Runge Kutta time stepping, (cf. Section 44), with time step k=h/10k=h/10 for which the temporal discretization error was negligible in comparison with the spatial error. We took a suitable right-hand side so that the exact solution of the system was η=exp⁡(2​t)​(cos⁡(π​x)+x+2)\eta=\exp(2t)(\cos(\pi x)+x+2), u=exp⁡(x​t)​(sin⁡(π​x)+x3−x2)u=\exp(xt)(\sin(\pi x)+x^{3}-x^{2}). The errors and orders of convergence produced by this numerical experiments are shown in Table 3.1. The rates are close to the theoretical predictions of Theorem 3.13.1. The table suggests that the L2L^{2} rate of convergence for η\eta is slightly less than 3.53.5, while that for uu is essentially four. It further suggests that ‖η−ηh‖1=O⁡(h2.5)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|_{1}=O(h^{2.5}), ‖u−uh‖1=O⁡(h3)\|u-u_{h}\|_{1}=O(h^{3}) (agreeing with the second estimate of (i)(i) of Theorem 3.13.1), ‖η−ηh‖∞=O⁡(h3)\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|_{\infty}=O(h^{3}) and ‖u−uh‖∞=O⁡(h4)\|u-u_{h}\|_{\infty}=O(h^{4}). We also mention that the W1,∞W^{1,\infty} orders of convergence (not shown here) were approximately equal to 2.22.2 for η\eta and 33 for uu, and that the convergence rates from a similar experiment with (CB)(\ref{cb}) were practically the same. In Figure 3.13.1 we plot the quantity κ:=‖η−ηh‖/(h3.5​ln⁡1/h)\kappa:=\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|/(h^{3.5}\sqrt{\ln 1/h}) as a function of N=1/hN=1/h; here ‖η−ηh‖\|\eta-\eta_{h}\| are the L2L^{2}-errors from Table 3.1. We observe that κ\kappa apparently approaches a constant close to 0.130.13 as NN grows, which seems to be consistent with the presence of a slow-varying modulation of h3.5h^{3.5} as h→0h\to 0, such as (ln⁡1/h)1/2(\ln 1/h)^{1/2}. We close this paragraph with a remark on the ‘effect of the boundary’ on the error estimates

of Theorem 3.13.1. The proofs of Lemma 3.43.4 and Theorem 3.13.1 suggest that the accuracy of ψ\psi in Lemma 3.43.4 and e.g. of ‖η−ηh‖\|\eta-\eta_{h}\| in Theorem 3.13.1 degenerates near the boundary of the interval. This is consistent with the results of the following numerical experiment. We integrated in time the (SCB)(\ref{scb}) system on [0,1][0,1] with suitable right-hand side and initial conditions so that the wave elevation is given by the travelling Gaussian profile η⁡(x,t)=0.5​exp⁡[−144​(x−0.5−0.2​t)2]\eta(x,t)=0.5\exp[-144(x-0.5-0.2t)^{2}] and the velocity by u⁡(x,t)=6​(η+1−1)​x​(x−1)u(x,t)=6(\sqrt{\eta+1}-1)x(x-1). (We use cubic splines in space and the explicit fourth-order RK scheme in time.) The support of the initial η\eta-profile is effectively contained in the interval [0.3,0.5][0.3,0.5] and the wave moves to the right and starts crossing the boundary at x=1x=1 at about t=1.5t=1.5 (see Figure 3.23.2).

In Table 3.2 we show the L2L^{2} errors of η\eta, as N=1/hN=1/h increases, at the temporal instances t=0.5t=0.5, 1.01.0, 1.51.5, 2.02.0 and 2.52.5. The rates of convergence are practically equal to four up to t=1.5t=1.5 but as η\eta becomes nonzero at the boundary they fall to a value consistent with the first inequality of (i)(i) of Theorem 3.13.1.

4. Fully discrete schemes

In this section we turn to the study of some temporal discretizations of the o.d.e. systems represented by the standard Galerkin spatial discretizations of (CB)(\ref{cb}) or (SCB)(\ref{scb}), such as (2.2)(\ref{eq22}) or (2.4)(\ref{eq24}), for example. We shall confine ourselves to explicit time stepping schemes in order to avoid the more costly implicit methods that require solving nonlinear systems of equations at each time step. Of course, with explicit methods there arises the issue of stability of the fully discrete schemes. We will not be exhaustive in our analysis but we will study as examples three simple, well known explicit Runge-Kutta temporal discretizations, that require, respectively, stability conditions of the type k=O⁡(h2)k=O(h^{2}), k=O⁡(h4/3)k=O(h^{4/3}), and k≤λ0​hk\leq\lambda_{0}h for λ0\lambda_{0} sufficiently small, where kk is the time step.

Lemma 4.1.

Suppose that the solution (η,u)(\eta,u) of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) is sufficiently smooth in [0,T][0,T]. Let H⁡(t)=Ih​η​(t)H(t)=I_{h}\eta(t), U⁡(t)=Ih,0​u​(t)U(t)=I_{h,0}u(t), and define ψ⁡(t)∈Sh2\psi(t)\in S_{h}^{2}, ζ⁡(t)∈Sh,02\zeta(t)\in S_{h,0}^{2} for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T by

Ht+P​Ux+12​P​(H​U)x\displaystyle H_{t}+PU_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}P(HU)_{x} =ψ,\displaystyle=\psi\,, (4.9)
Ut+A​Hx+32​A​(U​Ux)+12​A​(H​Hx)\displaystyle U_{t}+AH_{x}+\tfrac{3}{2}A(UU_{x})+\tfrac{1}{2}A(HH_{x}) =ζ.\displaystyle=\zeta\,. (4.10)

Then

‖ψ‖\displaystyle\|\psi\| ≤Ch3/2,∥ψt∥≤Ch3/2,\displaystyle\leq Ch^{3/2}\,,\quad\|\psi_{t}\|\leq Ch^{3/2}\,, (4.11)
‖ζ‖1\displaystyle\|\zeta\|_{1} ≤Ch2,∥ζt∥1≤Ch2,\displaystyle\leq Ch^{2}\,,\quad\,\,\,\,\|\zeta_{t}\|_{1}\leq Ch^{2}\,,

P⁡(ρt+[(1+12​η)​σ]x+12​(u​ρ)x−12​(ρ​σ)x)=−ψ.P\bigl(\rho_{t}+[(1+\tfrac{1}{2}\eta)\sigma]_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}(u\rho)_{x}-\tfrac{1}{2}(\rho\sigma)_{x}\bigr)=-\psi\,.

≤C⁡(‖σt‖+‖ρ‖+‖u​σ​‖+‖σ2‖+‖​η​ρ‖+‖ρ2‖)≤C​h2.\displaystyle\leq C(\|\sigma_{t}\|+\|\rho\|+\|u\sigma\|+\|\sigma^{2}\|+\|\eta\rho\|+\|\rho^{2}\|)\leq Ch^{2}\,.

We now proceed to prove error estimates for the explicit Euler-Galerkin schemes (4.7)(\ref{eq47}) and (4.8)(\ref{eq48}). We begin by a consistency result.

Lemma 4.2.

Suppose that the solution (η,u)(\eta,u) of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) is sufficiently smooth. Let Hn:=H⁡(tn)=Ih​η​(tn)H^{n}:=H(t^{n})=I_{h}\eta(t^{n}), Un=U⁡(tn)=Ih,0​u​(tn)U^{n}=U(t^{n})=I_{h,0}u(t^{n}), and define, for 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1, δ1n\delta_{1}^{n} and δ2n\delta_{2}^{n} by the equations

Then

max0≤n≤M−1⁡(‖δ1n‖+‖δ2n‖1)≤C​k​(k+h3/2).\max_{0\leq n\leq M-1}(\|\delta_{1}^{n}\|+\|\delta_{2}^{n}\|_{1})\leq Ck(k+h^{3/2})\,.

The analogous result holds for (CB)(\ref{cb}) as well.

Proof.

Using (4.9)(\ref{eq49}) and (4.10)(\ref{eq410}) we have, with ψn=ψ⁡(tn)\psi^{n}=\psi(t^{n}), ζn=ζ⁡(tn)\zeta^{n}=\zeta(t^{n}), that δ1n=Hn+1−Hn−k​Htn+k​ψn\delta_{1}^{n}=H^{n+1}-H^{n}-kH_{t}^{n}+k\psi^{n}, δ2n=Un+1−Un−k​Utn+k​ζn\delta_{2}^{n}=U^{n+1}-U^{n}-kU_{t}^{n}+k\zeta^{n}. Hence, for 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1,

by Taylor’s theorem and (4.11)(\ref{eq411}). ∎

Proposition 4.1.

Suppose that the solutions (η,u)(\eta,u) of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) and (CB)(\ref{cb}) are sufficiently smooth on [0,T][0,T]. Then, if μ=k/h2\mu=k/h^{2}, there is a constant C=C⁡(μ)C=C(\mu), which is an increasing continuous function of μ\mu, such that

max0≤n≤M⁡‖Hhn−η⁡(tn)‖≤C⁡(k+h3/2),max0≤n≤M⁡‖Uhn−u⁡(tn)‖1≤C⁡(k+h),\max_{0\leq n\leq M}\|H_{h}^{n}-\eta(t^{n})\|\leq C(k+h^{3/2})\,,\quad\max_{0\leq n\leq M}\|U_{h}^{n}-u(t^{n})\|_{1}\leq C(k+h)\,, (4.13)

where (Hhn,Uhn)(H_{h}^{n},U_{h}^{n}) satisfy (4.7)(\ref{eq47}) or (4.8)(\ref{eq48}) as the case may be.

(4.15)

It follows from (4.6)(\ref{eq46}) that

‖A​(Hn​εn)x‖1\displaystyle\|A(H^{n}\varepsilon^{n})_{x}\|_{1} ≤C​‖Hn​εn‖≤C​‖εn‖.\displaystyle\leq C\|H^{n}\varepsilon^{n}\|\leq C\|\varepsilon^{n}\|\,. (4.17)

Let now 0≤n∗≤M−10\leq n^{*}\leq M-1 be the maximal integer such that

≤C⁡(‖en‖1+‖en‖1​‖εn‖1)≤C​‖en‖1,\displaystyle\leq C(\|e^{n}\|_{1}+\|e^{n}\|_{1}\|\varepsilon^{n}\|_{1})\leq C\|e^{n}\|_{1}\,,

Remark 4.1.

The estimate (4.25)(\ref{eq425}) and Sobolev’s inequality imply that ‖en‖∞=O⁡(k+h3/2)\|e^{n}\|_{\infty}=O(k+h^{3/2}). Therefore, maxn⁡‖u⁡(tn)−Uhn‖∞=O⁡(k+h3/2)\max_{n}\|u(t^{n})-U_{h}^{n}\|_{\infty}=O(k+h^{3/2}).

Consider the linearized problem (2.43)(\ref{eq243}). In this case, the analogous fully discrete scheme is

As we saw in Proposition 4.14.1, when the nonlinear (CB)(\ref{cb}) or (SCB)(\ref{scb}) system is discetized by the explicit Euler-Galerkin method, the mesh condition k=O⁡(h2)k=O(h^{2}) is sufficient for stability. In a numerical experiment, we solved the nonlinear, nonhomogeneous (CB)(\ref{cb}) system using as exact solution η⁡(x,t)=exp⁡(2​t)​(cos⁡(π​x)+x+2)\eta(x,t)=\exp(2t)(\cos(\pi x)+x+2), u⁡(x,t)=exp⁡(x​t)​(sin⁡(π​x)+x3−x2)u(x,t)=\exp(xt)(\sin(\pi x)+x^{3}-x^{2}) for x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1], and discretizing by the explicit Euler-standard Galerkin method with piecewise linear functions and fixed N=1/h=400N=1/h=400. When we integrated up to T=1T=1 using k=h2k=h^{2}, we obtained an L2L^{2} error for η\eta that was approximately equal to 2.2090​(−4)2.2090(-4). The accuracy degenerated when we took k=hαk=h^{\alpha} with decreasing α<2\alpha<2. For example, at the temporal instance closest to T=1T=1 the computations yielded the following magnitudes of the L2L^{2} errors of η\eta:

  • k=h1.8k=h^{1.8}   3.8839​(−4)3.8839(-4)

  • k=h1.6k=h^{1.6}   1.1257​(−3)1.1257(-3)

  • k=h1.4k=h^{1.4}   3.6917​(−3)3.6917(-3)

  • k=h1.2k=h^{1.2}   overflow at about t=0.8t=0.8 .

for 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1, with Hh0=Ih​η0H_{h}^{0}=I_{h}\eta^{0}, Uh0=Ih,0​u0U_{h}^{0}=I_{h,0}u^{0}. In the case of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) the analogous equations are

Hhn,1\displaystyle H_{h}^{n,1} −Hhn+k2​P​Uh​xn+k4​P​(Hhn​Uhn)x=0,\displaystyle-H_{h}^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}PU_{hx}^{n}+\tfrac{k}{4}P(H_{h}^{n}U_{h}^{n})_{x}=0\,, (4.30)

In order to study the consistency and convergence of the schemes, we let again Hn=H⁡(tn)=Ih​η​(tn)H^{n}=H(t^{n})=I_{h}\eta(t^{n}), Un=U⁡(tn)=Ih,0​u​(tn)U^{n}=U(t^{n})=I_{h,0}u(t^{n}), where (η,u)(\eta,u) is the solution of (CB)(\ref{cb}) or (SCB)(\ref{scb}), and define, in the case of (SCB)(\ref{scb}), (Hn,1,Un,1)∈Sh2×Sh,02(H^{n,1},U^{n,1})\in S_{h}^{2}\times S_{h,0}^{2} for 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1 by the equations

In the case of (CB)(\ref{cb}) Hn,1H^{n,1}, Un,1U^{n,1} are defined analogously. Our consistency result is:

Lemma 4.3.

Suppose that the solution (η,u)(\eta,u) of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) is sufficiently smooth and let λ=k/h\lambda=k/h. Define, for 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1, δ1n\delta_{1}^{n}, δ2n\delta_{2}^{n} by the equations

δ1n\displaystyle\delta_{1}^{n} =Hn+1−Hn+k​P​Uxn,1+k2​P​(Hn,1​Un,1)x,\displaystyle=H^{n+1}-H^{n}+kPU_{x}^{n,1}+\tfrac{k}{2}P(H^{n,1}U^{n,1})_{x}\,, (4.32)
δ2n\displaystyle\delta_{2}^{n} =Un+1−Un+k​A​Hxn,1+3​k2​A​(Un,1​Uxn,1)+k2​A​(Hn,1​Hxn,1).\displaystyle=U^{n+1}-U^{n}+kAH_{x}^{n,1}+\tfrac{3k}{2}A(U^{n,1}U_{x}^{n,1})+\tfrac{k}{2}A(H^{n,1}H_{x}^{n,1})\,. (4.33)

Then, there exists a constant C1=C1​(λ)C_{1}=C_{1}(\lambda), which is a polynomial of λ\lambda of degree one, such that

max0≤n≤M−1⁡(‖δ1n‖+‖δ2n‖1)≤C1​k​(k2+h3/2).\max_{0\leq n\leq M-1}(\|\delta_{1}^{n}\|+\|\delta_{2}^{n}\|_{1})\leq C_{1}k(k^{2}+h^{3/2})\,.

The analogous result holds for (CB)(\ref{cb}) as well.

Proof.

Let 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1. By (4.31)(\ref{eq431}), (4.9)(\ref{eq49}) and (4.10)(\ref{eq410}) we have

Hn,1=Hn+k2​Htn−k2​ψn,Un,1=Un+k2​Utn−k2​ζn.H^{n,1}=H^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}H_{t}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}\psi^{n}\,,\quad U^{n,1}=U^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}U_{t}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}\zeta^{n}\,. (4.34)

From these expressions, after some algebra, we obtain

Hn,1​Un,1=Hn​Un+k2​(H​U)tn+w1n,H^{n,1}U^{n,1}=H^{n}U^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}(HU)_{t}^{n}+w_{1}^{n}\,,

where

w1n:=k24​Htn​Utn−k2​(Un+k2​Utn)​ψn−k2​(Hn+k2​Htn)​ζn+k24​ψn​ζn.w_{1}^{n}:=\tfrac{k^{2}}{4}H_{t}^{n}U_{t}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}(U^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}U_{t}^{n})\psi^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}(H^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}H_{t}^{n})\zeta^{n}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{4}\psi^{n}\zeta^{n}\,. (4.35)

Hence, by (4.32)(\ref{eq432}), (4.34)(\ref{eq434}), (4.9)(\ref{eq49}), and the above we obtain

δ1n=Hn+1−Hn−k​Htn−k22​Ht​tn+k​ψn+k22​ψtn−k22​P​ζxn+k2​P​w1​xn.\delta_{1}^{n}=H^{n+1}-H^{n}-kH_{t}^{n}-\tfrac{k^{2}}{2}H_{tt}^{n}+k\psi^{n}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{2}\psi_{t}^{n}-\tfrac{k^{2}}{2}P\zeta_{x}^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}Pw_{1x}^{n}\,. (4.36)

Now, (4.35)(\ref{eq435}), in view of (4.11)(\ref{eq411}) and the approximation and inverse properties of Sh2S_{h}^{2} and Sh,02S_{h,0}^{2}, gives

‖w1n‖1\displaystyle\|w_{1}^{n}\|_{1} ≤C⁡(k2​‖Htn‖1​‖Utn‖1+k​‖ψn‖1​(‖Un‖1+k​‖Utn‖1)CLOSE\displaystyle\leq C(k^{2}\|H_{t}^{n}\|_{1}\|U_{t}^{n}\|_{1}+k\|\psi^{n}\|_{1}(\|U^{n}\|_{1}+k\|U_{t}^{n}\|_{1})
OPEN+k​‖ζn‖1​(‖Hn‖1+k​‖Htn‖1)+k2​‖ψn‖1​‖ζn‖1)\displaystyle\qquad+k\|\zeta^{n}\|_{1}(\|H^{n}\|_{1}+k\|H_{t}^{n}\|_{1})+k^{2}\|\psi^{n}\|_{1}\|\zeta^{n}\|_{1})
≤c⁡(k2+k​h−1​h3/2​(1+c​k)+k​h2​(1+c​k)+k2​h−1​h7/2)\displaystyle\leq c(k^{2}+kh^{-1}h^{3/2}(1+ck)+kh^{2}(1+ck)+k^{2}h^{-1}h^{7/2})
≤c⁡(k2+λ​h3/2).\displaystyle\leq c(k^{2}+\lambda h^{3/2}).

Therefore, by Taylor’s theorem and (4.11)(\ref{eq411}) we have

‖δ1n‖≤c⁡(k3+k​h3/2+k2​h3/2+k2​h2+k⁡(k2+λ​h3/2)≤C1​k​(k2+h3/2)CLOSE,\|\delta_{1}^{n}\|\leq c(k^{3}+kh^{3/2}+k^{2}h^{3/2}+k^{2}h^{2}+k(k^{2}+\lambda h^{3/2})\leq C_{1}k(k^{2}+h^{3/2})\,, (4.37)

where C1C_{1} is a constant that is a polynomial of λ\lambda of degree one. (Such constants will be generically denoted by C1C_{1} in the sequel of this proof.) In order to estimate ‖δ2n‖1\|\delta_{2}^{n}\|_{1} note that by (4.34)(\ref{eq434})

Un,1​Uxn,1=Un​Uxn+k2​(U​Ux)tn+w2n,U^{n,1}U_{x}^{n,1}=U^{n}U_{x}^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}(UU_{x})_{t}^{n}+w_{2}^{n}\,, (4.38)

where

w2n:=k24​Utn​Ut​xn−k2​((Un+k2​Utn)​ζn)x+k24​ζn​ζxn.w_{2}^{n}:=\tfrac{k^{2}}{4}U_{t}^{n}U_{tx}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}\bigl((U^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}U_{t}^{n})\zeta^{n}\bigr)_{x}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{4}\zeta^{n}\zeta_{x}^{n}\,.

By (4.11)(\ref{eq411}) and the approximation properties of Sh,02S_{h,0}^{2} we have

‖w2n‖≤C⁡(k2+k​h2).\|w_{2}^{n}\|\leq C(k^{2}+kh^{2})\,. (4.39)

Similarly,

Hn,1​Hxn,1=Hn​Hxn+k2​(H​Hx)tn+w3n,H^{n,1}H_{x}^{n,1}=H^{n}H_{x}^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}(HH_{x})_{t}^{n}+w_{3}^{n}\,, (4.40)

where

w3n:=k24​Htn​Ht​xn−k2​((Hn+k2​Htn)​ψn)x+k24​ψn​ψxn.w_{3}^{n}:=\tfrac{k^{2}}{4}H_{t}^{n}H_{tx}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}\bigl((H^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}H_{t}^{n})\psi^{n}\bigr)_{x}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{4}\psi^{n}\psi_{x}^{n}\,.

By (4.11)(\ref{eq411}) and the approximation and inverse properties of Sh2S_{h}^{2} we have

‖w3n‖≤C⁡(k2+λ​h3/2).\|w_{3}^{n}\|\leq C(k^{2}+\lambda h^{3/2})\,. (4.41)

By (4.33)(\ref{eq433}), (4.35)(\ref{eq435}), (4.38)(\ref{eq438}), and (4.40)(\ref{eq440}), we see now that

δ2n=(Un+1−Un−k​Utn−k22​Ut​tn)+k​ζn+k22​ζtn−k22​A​ψxn+3​k2​A​w2n+k2​A​w3n.\delta_{2}^{n}=(U^{n+1}-U^{n}-kU_{t}^{n}-\tfrac{k^{2}}{2}U_{tt}^{n})+k\zeta^{n}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{2}\zeta_{t}^{n}-\tfrac{k^{2}}{2}A\psi_{x}^{n}+\tfrac{3k}{2}Aw_{2}^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}Aw_{3}^{n}\,.

Therefore, by Taylor’s theorem, (4.11)(\ref{eq411}), (4.6)(\ref{eq46}), (4.39)(\ref{eq439}), (4.41)(\ref{eq441}),

‖δ2n‖1≤c⁡(k3+k​h2+k2​h2+k2​h3/2+k3+k2​h2+k3+λ​k​h3/2)≤C1​k​(k2+h3/2),\|\delta_{2}^{n}\|_{1}\leq c(k^{3}+kh^{2}+k^{2}h^{2}+k^{2}h^{3/2}+k^{3}+k^{2}h^{2}+k^{3}+\lambda kh^{3/2})\leq C_{1}k(k^{2}+h^{3/2})\,,

which, with (4.37)(\ref{eq437}), concludes the proof of the Lemma. The case of (CB)(\ref{cb}) is entirely analogous. ∎

For the stability and convergence of the fully discrete scheme it does not suffice to suppose that k=O⁡(h)k=O(h). The following result shows that the stronger condition k=O⁡(h4/3)k=O(h^{4/3}) is sufficient.

Proposition 4.2.

Suppose that the solutions (η,u)(\eta,u) of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) and (CB)(\ref{cb}) are sufficiently smooth on [0,T][0,T]. Then, if μ=k/h4/3\mu=k/h^{4/3}, there is a constant C=C⁡(μ)C=C(\mu), which is an increasing continuous function of μ\mu, such that

max0≤n≤M⁡‖Hhn−η⁡(tn)‖≤C⁡(k2+h3/2),max0≤n≤M⁡‖Uhn−u⁡(tn)‖1≤C⁡(k2+h).\max_{0\leq n\leq M}\|H_{h}^{n}-\eta(t^{n})\|\leq C(k^{2}+h^{3/2})\,,\quad\max_{0\leq n\leq M}\|U_{h}^{n}-u(t^{n})\|_{1}\leq C(k^{2}+h)\,.

We consider (SCB)(\ref{scb}), and put εn=Hn−Hhn\varepsilon^{n}=H^{n}-H_{h}^{n}, en=Un−Uhne^{n}=U^{n}-U_{h}^{n}, θn=Hn,1−Hhn,1\theta^{n}=H^{n,1}-H_{h}^{n,1}, and ξn=Un,1−Uhn,1\xi^{n}=U^{n,1}-U_{h}^{n,1}. We will show that

max0≤n≤M⁡(‖εn‖+‖en‖1)≤C⁡(k2+h3/2),\max_{0\leq n\leq M}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})\leq C(k^{2}+h^{3/2})\,, (4.42)

from which the conclusion of the proposition follows. From (4.30)(\ref{eq430}), (4.32)(\ref{eq432}), (4.33)(\ref{eq433}) we have, for 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1

εn+1=εn−k​P​ξxn−k2​P​(Hn,1​Un,1−Hhn,1​Uhn,1)x+δ1n,\varepsilon^{n+1}=\varepsilon^{n}-kP\xi_{x}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}P(H^{n,1}U^{n,1}-H_{h}^{n,1}U_{h}^{n,1})_{x}+\delta_{1}^{n}\,, (4.43)

and

en+1=en−k​A​θxn−3​k2​A​(Un,1​Uxn,1−Uhn,1​Uh​xn,1)−k2​A​(Hn,1​Hxn,1−Hhn,1​Hh​xn,1)+δ2n.e^{n+1}=e^{n}-kA\theta_{x}^{n}-\tfrac{3k}{2}A(U^{n,1}U_{x}^{n,1}-U_{h}^{n,1}U_{hx}^{n,1})-\tfrac{k}{2}A(H^{n,1}H_{x}^{n,1}-H_{h}^{n,1}H_{hx}^{n,1})+\delta_{2}^{n}\,. (4.44)

From Lemma 4.34.3 we have an estimate of ‖δ1n‖+‖δ2n‖1\|\delta_{1}^{n}\|+\|\delta_{2}^{n}\|_{1}. Our goal is to obtain suitable estimates of the remaining terms of the right-hand sides of (4.43)(\ref{eq443}) and (4.44)(\ref{eq444}) in terms of ‖εn‖+‖en‖1\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1}. To do this, note first that (4.31)(\ref{eq431}) and (4.30)(\ref{eq430}) give

θn=εn−k2​P​exn−k4​P​(Hn​Un−Hhn​Uhn)x.\theta^{n}=\varepsilon^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}Pe_{x}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{4}P(H^{n}U^{n}-H_{h}^{n}U_{h}^{n})_{x}\,.

But Hn​Un−Hhn​Uhn=Hn​en−εn​en+Un​εnH^{n}U^{n}-H_{h}^{n}U_{h}^{n}=H^{n}e^{n}-\varepsilon^{n}e^{n}+U^{n}\varepsilon^{n}. Therefore

θn=εn−k4​ρ1n−k2​ω1n,\theta^{n}=\varepsilon^{n}-\tfrac{k}{4}\rho_{1}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}\omega_{1}^{n}\,, (4.45)

where

and

Similarly,

But Un​Uxn−Uh​Uh​xn=(Un​en)x−en​exnU^{n}U_{x}^{n}-U_{h}U_{hx}^{n}=(U^{n}e^{n})_{x}-e^{n}e_{x}^{n}, Hn​Hxn−Hhn​Hh​xn=(Hn​εn)x−εn​εxnH^{n}H_{x}^{n}-H_{h}^{n}H_{hx}^{n}=(H^{n}\varepsilon^{n})_{x}-\varepsilon^{n}\varepsilon_{x}^{n}. Therefore

where

In addition, by (4.45)(\ref{eq445}) we have

Hn,1​Un,1−Hhn,1​Uhn,1=Un​εn−k4​Un​ρ1n−k2​Un​ω1n+ω3n,H^{n,1}U^{n,1}-H_{h}^{n,1}U_{h}^{n,1}=U^{n}\varepsilon^{n}-\tfrac{k}{4}U^{n}\rho_{1}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}U^{n}\omega_{1}^{n}+\omega_{3}^{n}\,, (4.50)

where

From (4.43)(\ref{eq443}), (4.45)(\ref{eq445})-(4.50)(\ref{eq450}) we conclude therefore that for 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1

εn+1=εn−k2​ρ1n+k28​ρ2n−k​ω4n+δ1n,\varepsilon^{n+1}=\varepsilon^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}\rho_{1}^{n}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{8}\rho_{2}^{n}-k\omega_{4}^{n}+\delta_{1}^{n}\,, (4.52)

where

and

ω4n:=P​exn−k2​P​ω2​xn−k4​P​(Un​ω1n)x+12​P​ω3​xn.\omega_{4}^{n}:=Pe_{x}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}P\omega_{2x}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{4}P(U^{n}\omega_{1}^{n})_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}P\omega_{3x}^{n}\,. (4.54)

Finally, using the identities Un,1​Uxn,1−Uhn,1​Uh​xn,1=(Un,1​ξn)x−ξn​ξxnU^{n,1}U_{x}^{n,1}-U_{h}^{n,1}U_{hx}^{n,1}=(U^{n,1}\xi^{n})_{x}-\xi^{n}\xi_{x}^{n} and Hn,1​Hxn,1−Hhn,1​Hh​xn,1=(Hn,1​θn)x−θn​θxnH^{n,1}H_{x}^{n,1}-H_{h}^{n,1}H_{hx}^{n,1}=(H^{n,1}\theta^{n})_{x}-\theta^{n}\theta_{x}^{n}, we obtain from (4.44)(\ref{eq444}) that for 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1

en+1=en−k​A​θxn−3​k2​A​((Un,1​ξn)x−ξn​ξxn)−k2​A​((Hn,1​θn)x−θn​θxn)+δ2n.e^{n+1}=e^{n}-kA\theta_{x}^{n}-\tfrac{3k}{2}A\bigl((U^{n,1}\xi^{n})_{x}-\xi^{n}\xi_{x}^{n}\bigr)-\tfrac{k}{2}A\bigl((H^{n,1}\theta^{n})_{x}-\theta^{n}\theta_{x}^{n}\bigr)+\delta_{2}^{n}\,. (4.55)

‖εn‖1+‖en‖1≤1,0≤n≤n∗.\|\varepsilon^{n}\|_{1}+\|e^{n}\|_{1}\leq 1\,,\quad 0\leq n\leq n^{*}\,. (4.56)

Then, by (4.47)(\ref{eq447}), the approximation properties of Sh2S_{h}^{2} and (4.56)(\ref{eq456}), we have, for 0≤n≤n∗0\leq n\leq n^{*}

‖ω1n‖≤‖en‖1+C​‖Hn‖1​‖en‖1+C​‖εn‖1​‖en‖1≤C​‖en‖1.\|\omega_{1}^{n}\|\leq\|e^{n}\|_{1}+C\|H^{n}\|_{1}\|e^{n}\|_{1}+C\|\varepsilon^{n}\|_{1}\|e^{n}\|_{1}\leq C\|e^{n}\|_{1}\,. (4.57)

By (4.49)(\ref{eq449}), the approximation properties of Sh2S_{h}^{2}, Sh,02S_{h,0}^{2}, and (4.6)(\ref{eq46}) there follows for 0≤n≤n∗0\leq n\leq n^{*}

‖ω2n‖1≤C⁡(‖εn​‖+‖en‖+‖​en‖1​‖en​‖+‖εn‖+‖εn‖1‖​εn‖)≤C⁡(‖εn‖+‖en‖).\|\omega_{2}^{n}\|_{1}\leq C(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1}\|e^{n}\|+\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|\varepsilon^{n}\|_{1}\|\varepsilon^{n}\|)\leq C(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|)\,. (4.58)

Hence, by (4.48)(\ref{eq448}), for 0≤n≤n∗0\leq n\leq n^{*}

‖ξn‖1≤C⁡(‖εn‖+‖en‖1).\|\xi^{n}\|_{1}\leq C(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})\,. (4.59)

In addition, by (4.45)(\ref{eq445}), (4.46)(\ref{eq446}), (4.57)(\ref{eq457}) and the inverse assumptions we have for 0≤n≤n∗0\leq n\leq n^{*}

‖θn‖≤‖εn‖+C​k2​‖εn‖+C​‖en‖1≤(1+C​λ)|εn|+C​‖en‖1≤Cλ​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1),\|\theta^{n}\|\leq\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+C\tfrac{k}{2}\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+C\|e^{n}\|_{1}\leq(1+C\lambda)\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+C\|e^{n}\|_{1}\leq C_{\lambda}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})\,, (4.60)

where we have put again λ=k/h\lambda=k/h; in the sequel, CλC_{\lambda} will denote various constants that depend polynomially on λ\lambda. Note also that in view of (4.56)(\ref{eq456}) we have for 0≤n≤n∗0\leq n\leq n^{*}, from (4.57)(\ref{eq457}), (4.46)(\ref{eq446}) and inverse inequalities

‖θn‖1≤‖εn‖1+C​k​‖ρ1n‖1+C​k​‖ω1n‖1≤‖εn‖1+C​λ​‖ρ1n‖+C​λ​‖ω1n‖≤Cλ.\|\theta^{n}\|_{1}\leq\|\varepsilon^{n}\|_{1}+Ck\|\rho_{1}^{n}\|_{1}+Ck\|\omega_{1}^{n}\|_{1}\leq\|\varepsilon^{n}\|_{1}+C\lambda\|\rho_{1}^{n}\|+C\lambda\|\omega_{1}^{n}\|\leq C_{\lambda}\,. (4.61)

By (4.51)(\ref{eq451}), (4.34)(\ref{eq434}), (4.11)(\ref{eq411}), (4.60)(\ref{eq460}), (4.59)(\ref{eq459}) and (4.56)(\ref{eq456}) we have for 0≤n≤n∗0\leq n\leq n^{*}

‖ω3n‖\displaystyle\|\omega_{3}^{n}\| ≤C⁡(‖Un,1−Un‖1​‖θn‖+‖Hn,1‖​‖ξn‖1+‖θn‖​‖ξn‖1)\displaystyle\leq C(\|U^{n,1}-U^{n}\|_{1}\|\theta^{n}\|+\|H^{n,1}\|\|\xi^{n}\|_{1}+\|\theta^{n}\|\|\xi^{n}\|_{1}) (4.62)
≤C⁡((k+h2)​‖θn‖+‖ξn‖1+‖θn‖​‖ξn‖1)\displaystyle\leq C((k+h^{2})\|\theta^{n}\|+\|\xi^{n}\|_{1}+\|\theta^{n}\|\|\xi^{n}\|_{1})
≤Cλ​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1).\displaystyle\leq C_{\lambda}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})\,.

Also, by (4.60)(\ref{eq460}), (4.59)(\ref{eq459}), (4.61)(\ref{eq461}), for 0≤n≤n∗0\leq n\leq n^{*}

‖ω3n‖1\displaystyle\|\omega_{3}^{n}\|_{1} ≤C⁡(‖Un,1−Un‖1​‖θn‖1+‖Hn,1‖1​‖ξn‖1+‖θn‖1​‖ξn‖1)\displaystyle\leq C(\|U^{n,1}-U^{n}\|_{1}\|\theta^{n}\|_{1}+\|H^{n,1}\|_{1}\|\xi^{n}\|_{1}+\|\theta^{n}\|_{1}\|\xi^{n}\|_{1}) (4.63)
≤(k+h2)​h−1​Cλ​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1)+Cλ​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1)+Cλ​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1)\displaystyle\leq(k+h^{2})h^{-1}C_{\lambda}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})+C_{\lambda}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})+C_{\lambda}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})
≤Cλ​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1).\displaystyle\leq C_{\lambda}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})\,.

Hence, by (4.54)(\ref{eq454}), (4.58)(\ref{eq458}), (4.57)(\ref{eq457}), (4.62)(\ref{eq462}) and the inverse inequalities we have for 0≤n≤n∗0\leq n\leq n^{*}

‖ω4n‖≤‖en‖1+C​k​(‖εn‖+‖en‖)+C​λ​‖en‖1+Cλ​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1)≤Cλ​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1).\|\omega_{4}^{n}\|\leq\|e^{n}\|_{1}+Ck(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|)+C\lambda\|e^{n}\|_{1}+C_{\lambda}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})\leq C_{\lambda}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})\,.

‖−k​ω4n+δ1n‖≤Cλ​k​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1)+Cλ​k​(k+h3/2).\|-k\omega_{4}^{n}+\delta_{1}^{n}\|\leq C_{\lambda}k(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})+C_{\lambda}k(k+h^{3/2})\,. (4.64)

We embark now upon obtaining a sharp L2L^{2}-estimate of the remaining term εn−k2​ρ1n+k28​ρ2n\varepsilon^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}\rho_{1}^{n}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{8}\rho_{2}^{n} in (4.52)(\ref{eq452}). We have

‖εn−k2​ρ1n+k28​ρ2n‖2=‖εn‖2+k24​‖ρ1n‖2+k464​‖ρ2n‖2−k⁡(εn,ρ1n)+k24​(εn,ρ2n)−k38​(ρ1n,ρ2n).\|\varepsilon^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}\rho_{1}^{n}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{8}\rho_{2}^{n}\|^{2}=\|\varepsilon^{n}\|^{2}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{4}\|\rho_{1}^{n}\|^{2}+\tfrac{k^{4}}{64}\|\rho_{2}^{n}\|^{2}-k(\varepsilon^{n},\rho_{1}^{n})+\tfrac{k^{2}}{4}(\varepsilon^{n},\rho_{2}^{n})-\tfrac{k^{3}}{8}(\rho_{1}^{n},\rho_{2}^{n})\,.

Now, by (4.46)(\ref{eq446})

Also, by (4.53)(\ref{eq453}), (4.46)(\ref{eq446})

(εn,ρ2n)\displaystyle(\varepsilon^{n},\rho_{2}^{n}) =−(εxn,Un​ρ1n)=−‖ρ1n‖2+(Uxn​εn,ρ1n),\displaystyle=-(\varepsilon_{x}^{n},U^{n}\rho_{1}^{n})=-\|\rho_{1}^{n}\|^{2}+(U_{x}^{n}\varepsilon^{n},\rho_{1}^{n})\,,
(ρ1n,ρ2n)\displaystyle(\rho_{1}^{n},\rho_{2}^{n}) =12​(Uxn​ρ1n,ρ1n).\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(U_{x}^{n}\rho_{1}^{n},\rho_{1}^{n})\,.

We conclude that

‖εn−k2​ρ1n+k28​ρ2n‖2=‖εn‖2+k464​‖ρ2n‖2−k2​(Uxn​εn,εn)+k24​(Uxn​εn,ρ1n)−k316​(Uxn​ρ1n,ρ1n).\|\varepsilon^{n}-\tfrac{k}{2}\rho_{1}^{n}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{8}\rho_{2}^{n}\|^{2}=\|\varepsilon^{n}\|^{2}+\tfrac{k^{4}}{64}\|\rho_{2}^{n}\|^{2}-\tfrac{k}{2}(U_{x}^{n}\varepsilon^{n},\varepsilon^{n})+\tfrac{k^{2}}{4}(U_{x}^{n}\varepsilon^{n},\rho_{1}^{n})-\tfrac{k^{3}}{16}(U_{x}^{n}\rho_{1}^{n},\rho_{1}^{n})\,. (4.65)

≤‖en‖1+Cλ​k​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1)+Cλ​k​(k2+h3/2).\displaystyle\leq\|e^{n}\|_{1}+C_{\lambda}k(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})+C_{\lambda}k(k^{2}+h^{3/2})\,.

Remark 4.3.

Arguing as in Remark 4.14.1 we have again ‖Uhn−u⁡(tn)‖∞=O⁡(k2+h3/2)\|U_{h}^{n}-u(t^{n})\|_{\infty}=O(k^{2}+h^{3/2}).

Remark 4.4.

If we repeat the numerical experiment in Remark 4.24.2 using the improved Euler method for time stepping, we obtain, for N=1/h=400N=1/h=400, the evolution of the L2L^{2} errors ‖Hhn−η⁡(tn)‖\|H_{h}^{n}-\eta(t^{n})\| when k=hk=h and k=h4/3k=h^{4/3} shown in Table 4.1. These results suggest that the condition k=h4/3k=h^{4/3} is probably necessary as well for the stability of the scheme. If we repeat the experiment using k=hk=h and the fourth-order explicit classical R-K scheme for time stepping (this scheme, as will be shown in the next paragraph, is stable when k=hk=h,) we obtain errors approximately equal to those of the last column of Table 4.1: For example at tn=0.95t^{n}=0.95 and tn=1.0t^{n}=1.0 the analogous errors are equal to 0.1810​(−3)0.1810(-3) and 0.1954​(−3)0.1954(-3), respectively. This implies that the errors of the last column of Table 4.1 are essentially due to the spatial discretization.

4.3. Fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme with cubic splines

Our third example is time stepping with the classical, fourth-order accurate four-stage explicit Runge-Kutta scheme, written in the case of the o.d.e. y′=f⁡(t,y)y^{\prime}=f(t,y) in the three-step form

yn,1\displaystyle y^{n,1} =yn+k2​f​(tn+k2,yn),\displaystyle=y^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}f(t^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2},y^{n})\,,
yn,2\displaystyle y^{n,2} =yn+k2​f​(tn+k2,yn,1),\displaystyle=y^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2}f(t^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2},y^{n,1})\,,
yn,3\displaystyle y^{n,3} =yn+k​f​(tn+k,yn,2),\displaystyle=y^{n}+kf(t^{n}+k,y^{n,2})\,,
yn+1\displaystyle y^{n+1} =yn+k⁡(16​f​(tn,yn)+13​f​(tn+k2,yn,1)+13​f​(tn+k2,yn,2)+16​f​(tn+k,yn,3)).\displaystyle=y^{n}+k\bigl(\tfrac{1}{6}f(t^{n},y^{n})+\tfrac{1}{3}f(t^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2},y^{n,1})+\tfrac{1}{3}f(t^{n}+\tfrac{k}{2},y^{n,2})+\tfrac{1}{6}f(t^{n}+k,y^{n,3})\bigr)\,.

We will couple this scheme with a space discretization that uses cubic splines on a uniform mesh on [0,1][0,1]. We recall that the semidiscrete problem can be written, e.g. in the case of the (SCB)(\ref{scb}), in the form (3.8)(\ref{eq38}) or, equivalently, as follows. We seek (ηh,uh)(\eta_{h},u_{h}) ∈C1​(0,T,Sh4×Sh,04)\in C^{1}(0,T;S_{h}^{4}\times S_{h,0}^{4}) such that

ηh​t+P​uh​x+12​P​(ηh​uh)x=0,uh​t+A​ηh​x+32​A​(uh​uh​x)+12​A​(ηh​ηh​x)=0,0≤t≤T,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \eta_{ht}&+Pu_{hx}+\tfrac{1}{2}P(\eta_{h}u_{h})_{x}=0\,,\\ u_{ht}&+A\eta_{hx}+\tfrac{3}{2}A(u_{h}u_{hx})+\tfrac{1}{2}A(\eta_{h}\eta_{hx})=0\,,\end{aligned}\quad 0\leq t\leq T\,, (4.69)
ηh(0)=Ihη0,uh(0)=Rhu0,\displaystyle\eta_{h}(0)=I_{h}\eta_{0}\,,\quad u_{h}(0)=R_{h}u_{0}\,,

where P:L2→Sh4P:L^{2}\to S_{h}^{4} is the L2L^{2}-projection operator onto Sh4S_{h}^{4}, A:L2→Sh,04A:L^{2}\to S_{h,0}^{4} is defined as in (4.5)(\ref{eq45}), but now in Sh,04S_{h,0}^{4}, IhI_{h} is the interpolant in Sh4S_{h}^{4}, and RhR_{h} is introduced in Paragraph 3.13.1. We start with an estimation of the truncation errors of the semidiscrete equations when applied to Ih​η​(t)I_{h}\eta(t) and Rh​u​(t)R_{h}u(t) similar to that of Lemma 4.14.1.

Lemma 4.4.

Suppose that the solution (ηh,uh)(\eta_{h},u_{h}) of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) is sufficiently smooth in [0,T][0,T]. Let H⁡(t)=Ih​η​(t)H(t)=I_{h}\eta(t), U⁡(t)=Rh​u​(t)U(t)=R_{h}u(t) and define ψ=ψ⁡(t)∈Sh4\psi=\psi(t)\in S_{h}^{4}, ζ=ζ⁡(t)∈Sh,04\zeta=\zeta(t)\in S_{h,0}^{4}, for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T by

Ht+P​Ux+12​P​(H​U)x\displaystyle H_{t}+PU_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}P(HU)_{x} =ψ,\displaystyle=\psi\,, (4.70)
Ut+A​Hx+32​A​(U​Ux)+12​A​(H​Hx)\displaystyle U_{t}+AH_{x}+\tfrac{3}{2}A(UU_{x})+\tfrac{1}{2}A(HH_{x}) =ζ.\displaystyle=\zeta\,. (4.71)

Then, for j=0j=0, 11, 22, 33

‖∂tjψ‖≤C​h3.5​ln⁡1/h,‖∂tjζ‖1≤C​h4,\|\partial_{t}^{j}\psi\|\leq Ch^{3.5}\sqrt{\ln 1/h}\,,\qquad\|\partial_{t}^{j}\zeta\|_{1}\leq Ch^{4}\,, (4.72)

Proof.

Ht+P​Ux+12​P​(H​U)x\displaystyle H_{t}+PU_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}P(HU)_{x} =ψ,\displaystyle=\psi\,,

P​ρt+P​σx+12​P​(η​u−H​U)x=−ψ.P\rho_{t}+P\sigma_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}P(\eta u-HU)_{x}=-\psi\,.

Since

η​u−H​U=η⁡(u−U)+U⁡(η−H)=η⁡(u−U)−(u−U)​(η−H)+u⁡(η−H)=η​σ+u​ρ−ρ​σ,\eta u-HU=\eta(u-U)+U(\eta-H)=\eta(u-U)-(u-U)(\eta-H)+u(\eta-H)=\eta\sigma+u\rho-\rho\sigma\,,

A⁡(ut−13​ut​x​x)=Ut.A(u_{t}-\tfrac{1}{3}u_{txx})=U_{t}\,.

Subtracting now the equations

We show stability and convergence of the fully discrete scheme in the course of the proof of the following result.

Proposition 4.3.

Suppose that the solution (η,u)(\eta,u) of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) is sufficiently smooth on [0,T][0,T]. Let λ=k/h\lambda=k/h and (Hhn,Uhn)(H_{h}^{n},U_{h}^{n}) be the solution of (4.73)(\ref{eq473})-(4.74)(\ref{eq474}). Then, there exists a positive constant λ0\lambda_{0} and a constant CC independent of kk and h, such that for λ≤λ0\lambda\leq\lambda_{0},

max0≤n≤M⁡‖η⁡(tn)−Hhn‖≤C⁡(k4+h3.5​ln⁡1/h),max0≤n≤M⁡‖u⁡(tn)−Uhn‖1≤C⁡(k4+h3).\max_{0\leq n\leq M}\|\eta(t^{n})-H_{h}^{n}\|\leq C(k^{4}+h^{3.5}\sqrt{\ln 1/h})\,,\qquad\quad\max_{0\leq n\leq M}\|u(t^{n})-U_{h}^{n}\|_{1}\leq C(k^{4}+h^{3})\,.
Proof.

It suffices to show that

max0≤n≤M⁡(‖Hn−Hhn‖+‖Un−Uhn‖1)≤C⁡(k4+h3.5​ln⁡1/h).\max_{0\leq n\leq M}(\|H^{n}-H_{h}^{n}\|+\|U^{n}-U_{h}^{n}\|_{1})\leq C(k^{4}+h^{3.5}\sqrt{\ln 1/h})\,.

Let

εn=Hn−Hhn,en=Un−Uhn,εn,j=Vn,j−Hhn,j,en,j=Wn,j−Uhn,j,j=1,2,3.\varepsilon^{n}=H^{n}-H_{h}^{n}\,,\quad e^{n}=U^{n}-U_{h}^{n}\,,\quad\varepsilon^{n,j}=V^{n,j}-H_{h}^{n,j}\,,\quad e^{n,j}=W^{n,j}-U_{h}^{n,j}\,,\quad j=1,2,3\,.

Then, by (4.75)(\ref{eq475}) and (4.78)(\ref{eq478}), we have for j=1,2,3j=1,2,3

εn,j=εn−k​aj​P​(Φn,j−1−Φhn,j−1)x,\varepsilon^{n,j}=\varepsilon^{n}-ka_{j}P\bigl(\Phi^{n,j-1}-\Phi_{h}^{n,j-1}\bigr)_{x}\,, (4.99)
en,j=en−k​aj​A​(Fn,j−1−Fhn,j−1),e^{n,j}=e^{n}-ka_{j}A\bigl(F^{n,j-1}-F_{h}^{n,j-1}\bigr)\,, (4.100)

and by (4.79)(\ref{eq479}), (4.81)(\ref{eq481}), and (4.82)(\ref{eq482})

εn+1=εn−k​∑j=14bj​P​(Φn,j−1−Φhn,j−1)x+δ1n,\varepsilon^{n+1}=\varepsilon^{n}-k\sum_{j=1}^{4}b_{j}P\bigl(\Phi^{n,j-1}-\Phi_{h}^{n,j-1}\bigr)_{x}+\delta_{1}^{n}\,, (4.101)
en+1=en−k​∑j=14bj​A​(Fn,j−1−Fhn,j−1)+δ2n.e^{n+1}=e^{n}-k\sum_{j=1}^{4}b_{j}A\bigl(F^{n,j-1}-F_{h}^{n,j-1}\bigr)+\delta_{2}^{n}\,. (4.102)

We embark upon the proof by deriving suitable estimates for εn,1\varepsilon^{n,1} and en,1e^{n,1}. To this end, putting Φhn:=Φhn,0\Phi_{h}^{n}:=\Phi_{h}^{n,0}, we have

Φn−Φhn=en+12​(Hn​Un−Hhn​Uhn),\Phi^{n}-\Phi_{h}^{n}=e^{n}+\tfrac{1}{2}(H^{n}U^{n}-H_{h}^{n}U_{h}^{n})\,,

and since

Hn​Un−Hhn​Uhn\displaystyle H^{n}U^{n}-H_{h}^{n}U_{h}^{n} =Hn​(Un−Uhn)−(Un−Uhn)​(Hn−Hhn)+Un​(Hn−Hhn)\displaystyle=H^{n}(U^{n}-U_{h}^{n})-(U^{n}-U_{h}^{n})(H^{n}-H_{h}^{n})+U^{n}(H^{n}-H_{h}^{n})
=Hn​en−εn​en+Un​εn,\displaystyle=H^{n}e^{n}-\varepsilon^{n}e^{n}+U^{n}\varepsilon^{n}\,,

we will have

Φn−Φhn=en+12​(Hn​en−εn​en)+12​Un​εn,\Phi^{n}-\Phi_{h}^{n}=e^{n}+\tfrac{1}{2}(H^{n}e^{n}-\varepsilon^{n}e^{n})+\tfrac{1}{2}U^{n}\varepsilon^{n}\,,

i.e.

where

P​(Φn−Φhn)x=γ1n+12​ρ1n,P(\Phi^{n}-\Phi_{h}^{n})_{x}=\gamma_{1}^{n}+\tfrac{1}{2}\rho_{1}^{n}\,, (4.103)

Let 0≤n∗≤M−10\leq n^{*}\leq M-1 be the maximal integer for which

‖εn‖1+‖en‖1≤1,0≤n≤n∗.\|\varepsilon^{n}\|_{1}+\|e^{n}\|_{1}\leq 1\,,\qquad 0\leq n\leq n^{*}\,.

and also

In order to estimate en,1e^{n,1} we note, setting Fhn=Fhn,0F_{h}^{n}=F_{h}^{n,0}, that

Since

=(Un​en)x−en​exn,\displaystyle=(U^{n}e^{n})_{x}-e^{n}e_{x}^{n}\,,

and

Recalling the expression for en,1e^{n,1} in (4.101)(\ref{eq4101}) we have for n≤n∗n\leq n^{*}

‖en,1‖1≤C⁡(‖εn‖+‖en‖1).\|e^{n,1}\|_{1}\leq C(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})\,. (4.110)

We now turn to deriving estimates for εn,2\varepsilon^{n,2} and en,2e^{n,2}. With this aim in mind, we note for later reference that it follows from the definition of Vn,jV^{n,j}, Wn,jW^{n,j}, Fn,jF^{n,j} that for 0≤n≤M−10\leq n\leq M-1, j=0,1,2,3j=0,1,2,3

‖Vn,j‖1+‖Wn,j‖1≤Cλ,‖Fn,j‖−1≤Cλ.\|V^{n,j}\|_{1}+\|W^{n,j}\|_{1}\leq C_{\lambda}\,,\qquad\|F^{n,j}\|_{-1}\leq C_{\lambda}\,.

Since now

Φn,1−Φhn,1=en,1+12​(Vn,1​Wn,1−Hhn,1​Uhn,1),\Phi^{n,1}-\Phi_{h}^{n,1}=e^{n,1}+\tfrac{1}{2}(V^{n,1}W^{n,1}-H_{h}^{n,1}U_{h}^{n,1})\,,

and

Vn,1​Wn,1−Hhn,1​Uhn,1\displaystyle V^{n,1}W^{n,1}-H_{h}^{n,1}U_{h}^{n,1} =Vn,1​(Wn,1−Uhn,1)−(Wn,1−Uhn,1)​(Vn,1−Hhn,1)+Wn,1​(Vn,1−Hhn,1)\displaystyle=V^{n,1}(W^{n,1}-U_{h}^{n,1})-(W^{n,1}-U_{h}^{n,1})(V^{n,1}-H_{h}^{n,1})+W^{n,1}(V^{n,1}-H_{h}^{n,1})
=Vn,1​en,1−en,1​εn,1+Wn,1​εn,1,\displaystyle=V^{n,1}e^{n,1}-e^{n,1}\varepsilon^{n,1}+W^{n,1}\varepsilon^{n,1}\,,

using (4.80)(\ref{eq480}) we have by (4.105)(\ref{eq4105})

Wn,1​εn,1\displaystyle W^{n,1}\varepsilon^{n,1} =(Un−a1​k​A​Fn)​(εn−a1​k​γ1n−a1​k2​ρ1n)\displaystyle=(U^{n}-a_{1}kAF^{n})(\varepsilon^{n}-a_{1}k\gamma_{1}^{n}-\tfrac{a_{1}k}{2}\rho_{1}^{n})
=Un​εn−a1​k2​Un​ρ1n−a1​k​Un​γ1n−a1​k​(A​Fn)​εn,1,\displaystyle=U^{n}\varepsilon^{n}-\tfrac{a_{1}k}{2}U^{n}\rho_{1}^{n}-a_{1}kU^{n}\gamma_{1}^{n}-a_{1}k(AF^{n})\varepsilon^{n,1}\,,

γ~2n=en,1+12​Vn,1​en,1−12​en,1​εn,1−a1​k2​Un​γ1n−a1​k2​(A​Fn)​εn,1.\widetilde{\gamma}_{2}^{n}=e^{n,1}+\tfrac{1}{2}V^{n,1}e^{n,1}-\tfrac{1}{2}e^{n,1}\varepsilon^{n,1}-\tfrac{a_{1}k}{2}U^{n}\gamma_{1}^{n}-\tfrac{a_{1}k}{2}(AF^{n})\varepsilon^{n,1}\,. (4.111)

‖γ2n‖≤Cλ​(‖εn‖+‖en‖1),\|\gamma_{2}^{n}\|\leq C_{\lambda}(\|\varepsilon^{n}\|+\|e^{n}\|_{1})\,, (4.114)

holds for n≤n∗n\leq n^{*}. Now, by (4.80)(\ref{eq480}) and (4.78)(\ref{eq478})

εn,2=Vn,2−Hhn,2=εn−a2​k​P​(Φn,1−Φhn,1)x,\varepsilon^{n,2}=V^{n,2}-H_{h}^{n,2}=\varepsilon^{n}-a_{2}kP(\Phi^{n,1}-\Phi_{h}^{n,1})_{x}\,,

we have by (4.117)(\ref{eq4117}) for n≤n∗n\leq n^{*}

Hence, by (4.104)(\ref{eq4104}), (4.113)(\ref{eq4113}), and (4.132)(\ref{eq4132}) we obtain

P​(Φn,3−Φhn,3)x=12​ρ1n−k4​ρ2n+a2​k28​ρ3n−a1​a2​k316​ρ4n+γ4n,P(\Phi^{n,3}-\Phi_{h}^{n,3})_{x}=\tfrac{1}{2}\rho_{1}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{4}\rho_{2}^{n}+\tfrac{a_{2}k^{2}}{8}\rho_{3}^{n}-\tfrac{a_{1}a_{2}k^{3}}{16}\rho_{4}^{n}+\gamma_{4}^{n}\,, (4.131)

By (4.130)(\ref{eq4130}) and (4.126)(\ref{eq4126}) we obtain for n≤n∗n\leq n^{*}

‖γ~4n‖1≤Cλ​‖en,3‖1+C​k​‖γ3n‖1+Cλ​k​‖εn,3‖1,\|\widetilde{\gamma}_{4}^{n}\|_{1}\leq C_{\lambda}\|e^{n,3}\|_{1}+Ck\|\gamma_{3}^{n}\|_{1}+C_{\lambda}k\|\varepsilon^{n,3}\|_{1}\,,

From (4.103)(\ref{eq4103}) and (4.112)(\ref{eq4112}) we obtain

b1​P​(Φn−Φhn)x+b2​P​(Φn,1−Φhn,1)x\displaystyle b_{1}P(\Phi^{n}-\Phi_{h}^{n})_{x}+b_{2}P(\Phi^{n,1}-\Phi_{h}^{n,1})_{x} =12​(b1+b2)​ρ1n−a1​b2​k4​ρ2n+b1​γ1+b2​γ2\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(b_{1}+b_{2})\rho_{1}^{n}-\tfrac{a_{1}b_{2}k}{4}\rho_{2}^{n}+b_{1}\gamma_{1}+b_{2}\gamma_{2}
=14​ρ1n−k24​ρ2n+16​γ1n+13​γ2n.\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{4}\rho_{1}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{24}\rho_{2}^{n}+\tfrac{1}{6}\gamma_{1}^{n}+\tfrac{1}{3}\gamma_{2}^{n}\,.

From (4.121)(\ref{eq4121}) and (4.131)(\ref{eq4131}) we see that

−b4​a1​a2​k316​ρ4n+b3​γ3n+b4​γ4n\displaystyle\qquad-\tfrac{b_{4}a_{1}a_{2}k^{3}}{16}\rho_{4}^{n}+b_{3}\gamma_{3}^{n}+b_{4}\gamma_{4}^{n}
=14​ρ1n−k12​ρ2n+k248​ρ3n−k324⋅16​ρ4n+13​γ3n+16​γ4n.\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{4}\rho_{1}^{n}-\tfrac{k}{12}\rho_{2}^{n}+\tfrac{k^{2}}{48}\rho_{3}^{n}-\tfrac{k^{3}}{24\cdot 16}\rho_{4}^{n}+\tfrac{1}{3}\gamma_{3}^{n}+\tfrac{1}{6}\gamma_{4}^{n}\,.

Therefore, in view of (4.101)(\ref{eq4101}), we have

for n≤n∗n\leq n^{*}. We begin now the estimation of

5. A non-standard Galerkin method

In this section we analyze a semidiscrete Galerkin approximation of (CB)(\ref{cb}) and (SCB)(\ref{scb}) which is non-standard in the sense that it approximates η\eta by piecewise linear, continuous functions and uu by piecewise quadratic, C01C_{0}^{1} functions, defined on the same mesh. (The method may be generalized using the analogous pairs of higher-order splines but here we confine ourselves to the low-order case.) In the analysis, we consider only the uniform mesh case, where a series of superaccuracy results for the error of the L2L^{2}-projection onto the space of piecewise linear continuous functions affords proving optimal-order error estimates.

5.1. Preliminaries and the basic results

Using the notation of paragraph 2.22.2, in addition to Sh2S_{h}^{2} we let

Sh,03:={ϕ∈C1:ϕ|[xj,xj+1]∈ℙ2,  1≤j≤N,ϕ(0)=ϕ(1)=0}.S_{h,0}^{3}:=\{\phi\in C^{1}:\phi\big|_{[x_{j},x_{j+1}]}\in\mathbb{P}_{2}\,,\,\,1\leq j\leq N\,,\,\,\phi(0)=\phi(1)=0\}\,.

(ηh​t,ϕ)+(uh​x,ϕ)+12​((ηh​uh)x,ϕ)\displaystyle(\eta_{ht},\phi)+(u_{hx},\phi)+\tfrac{1}{2}((\eta_{h}u_{h})_{x},\phi) =0,∀ϕ∈Sh2\displaystyle=0\,,\quad\forall\phi\in S_{h}^{2} (5.1)
a⁡(uh​t,χ)+(ηh​x,χ)+32​(uh​uh​x,χ)+12​(ηh​ηh​x,χ)\displaystyle a(u_{ht},\chi)+(\eta_{hx},\chi)+\tfrac{3}{2}(u_{h}u_{hx},\chi)+\tfrac{1}{2}(\eta_{h}\eta_{hx},\chi) =0,∀χ∈Sh,03\displaystyle=0\,,\quad\forall\chi\in S_{h,0}^{3} (5.2)

and

‖ηh​(t)‖2+‖uh​(t)‖12=‖ηh​(0)‖2+‖uh​(0)‖12,\|\eta_{h}(t)\|^{2}+\|u_{h}(t)\|_{1}^{2}=\|\eta_{h}(0)\|^{2}+\|u_{h}(0)\|_{1}^{2}\,, (5.4)

The plan of the section is as follows: We will start by stating the preliminary Lemmas 5.15.1-5.45.4 with the aid of which we will prove our main error estimate, Theorem 5.15.1. Let η∈C1\eta\in C^{1} and u∈C03u\in C_{0}^{3}. If σ=u−Rh​u\sigma=u-R_{h}u and ζ∈Sh2\zeta\in S_{h}^{2} is such that

With the aid of these lemmas we may establish the basic result of this section:

Theorem 5.1.

Suppose that the solution (η,u)(\eta,u) of (SCB)(\ref{scb}) is such that η∈C⁡(0,T,C4)\eta\in C(0,T;C^{4}), ηt∈C⁡(0,T,C2)\eta_{t}\in C(0,T;C^{2}), uu, ut∈C⁡(0,T,C03)u_{t}\in C(0,T;C_{0}^{3}) and let (ηh,uh)(\eta_{h},u_{h}) be the solution of the semidiscrete problem (5.1)(\ref{eq51})-(5.3)(\ref{eq53}). Then

(i)\displaystyle(i)\,\,\,\,\, max0≤t≤T⁡(‖u⁡(t)−uh​(t)‖+h​‖η⁡(t)−ηh​(t)‖)≤C​h3,\displaystyle\max_{0\leq t\leq T}(\|u(t)-u_{h}(t)\|+h\|\eta(t)-\eta_{h}(t)\|)\leq Ch^{3}\,,

5.3. Numerical experiments

We considered first the (CB)(\ref{cb}) system, that we discretized by the nonstandard method analyzed in the previous two sections using the subspaces Sh2S_{h}^{2} and Sh,03S_{h,0}^{3} for approximating η\eta and uu, respectively. (We considered the nonhomogeneous system with a suitable right-hand side so that the solution is η=exp⁡(2​t)​(cos⁡(π​x)+x2+2)\eta=\exp(2t)(\cos(\pi x)+x^{2}+2), u=exp⁡(x​t)​(sin⁡(π​x)+x3−x2)u=\exp(xt)(\sin(\pi x)+x^{3}-x^{2}).) We integrated the semidiscrete system up to T=1T=1 by the fourth-order accurate explicit Runge-Kutta method analyzed in paragraph 4.34.3 with time step k=h/10k=h/10; the temporal discretization error was negligible in comparison to the spatial error.

Table 5.1 shows the resulting errors and orders of convergence in various norms. The optimal-order L2L^{2}- and L∞L^{\infty} rates of convergence of Theorem 5.15.1 are confirmed and the H1H^{1} rates are as expected. We obtained the same rates for the (SCB)(\ref{scb}) system. Table 5.2 shows the analogous errors and rates

of convergence for the same problem but now discretized so that ηh∈Sh3\eta_{h}\in S_{h}^{3}, i.e. in the space of C1C^{1} quadratic splines, and uh∈Sh,04u_{h}\in S_{h,0}^{4}, i.e. in the space of cubic splines that vanish at x=0x=0 and at x=1x=1. We observe e.g. that the associated L2L^{2}-rates of convergence for this higher order pair of subspaces are, as expected, equal to 33 for η\eta and 44 for uu. The (SCB)(\ref{scb}) system gave the same results.

The error analysis in paragraphs 5.15.1 and 5.25.2 depended strongly on the assumption of uniform mesh. In the case of nonuniform mesh we expect some order reduction. For example, Table 5.3 shows the L2L^{2} errors and orders of convergence that we obtained for (CB)(\ref{cb}) by approximating (ηh,uh)(\eta_{h},u_{h}) in Sh2×Sh,03S_{h}^{2}\times S_{h,0}^{3} and using for both subspaces the exact solution and the nonuniform mesh with which Table 2.3(a) was produced. Both rates are apparently reduced by one now.

6. Remarks on standard Galerkin methods for related hyperbolic problems

We conclude the paper with a section of remarks on the application of standard Galerkin methods on some simple first-order hyperbolic problems. Our aim is to show examples of such problems in which the techniques previously developed in this paper may be applied to some advantage.

6.1. Initial-boundary-value problem for a single hyperbolic equation

For T>0T>0 consider the initial-boundary-value problem

ηt+ηx=0,    0≤x≤1,0≤t≤T,\displaystyle\eta_{t}+\eta_{x}=0\,,\qquad\,\,\,\,0\leq x\leq 1\,,\quad 0\leq t\leq T\,, (6.1)
η(x,0)=η0(x),0≤x≤1,\displaystyle\eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\,,\quad 0\leq x\leq 1\,,
η(0,t)=0,0≤t≤T.\displaystyle\eta(0,t)=0\,,\qquad\quad 0\leq t\leq T\,.

It is clear that if η0∈Ck\eta_{0}\in C^{k}, for integer k≥0k\geq 0, and η0(j)​(0)=0\eta_{0}^{(j)}(0)=0, j=0,…,kj=0,\dots,k, then (6.1)(\ref{eq61}) possesses a unique solution η\eta given for (x,t)∈[0,1]×[0,T](x,t)\in[0,1]\times[0,T] by

η⁡(x,t)={η0​(x−t),x>t,0,x<t.\eta(x,t)=\begin{cases}\eta_{0}(x-t)&,\quad x>t\,,\\ 0&,\quad x<t\,.\end{cases}

The solution is classical if k≥1k\geq 1 and, for example, has the property that η⁡(⋅,t)∈Ck\eta(\cdot,t)\in C^{k} for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. For integer N≥2N\geq 2 and h=1/Nh=1/N we consider the uniform mesh given by xi=i​hx_{i}=ih, i=0,1,…,Ni=0,1,\dots,N, and put Ij=[xj−1,xj]I_{j}=[x_{j-1},x_{j}]. We let

Sh2∘ ={ϕ∈C[0,1]:ϕ|Ij∈ℙ1,  1≤j≤N,ϕ(0)=0},S_{h}^{2}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 7.3194pt\hbox{\scriptsize$\circ$}\enskip}=\{\phi\in C[0,1]:\phi\big|_{I_{j}}\in\mathbb{P}_{1},\,\,1\leq j\leq N,\,\,\phi(0)=0\}\,,

and denote by {ϕj}j=1N\{\phi_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} the basis of Sh2​∘ S_{h}^{2}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 7.3194pt\hbox{\scriptsize$\circ$}\enskip} with the property that ϕi​(xj)=δi​j\phi_{i}(x_{j})=\delta_{ij}. The standard Galerkin method for (6.1)(\ref{eq61}) may be then defined as follows: We seek ηh:[0,T]→Sh2​∘ \eta_{h}:[0,T]\to S_{h}^{2}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 7.3194pt\hbox{\scriptsize$\circ$}\enskip}, such that

(ηh​t,ϕ)+(ηh​x,ϕ)=0,∀ϕ∈Sh2∘ ,  0≤t≤T,\displaystyle(\eta_{ht},\phi)+(\eta_{hx},\phi)=0\,,\quad\forall\phi\in S_{h}^{2}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 7.3194pt\hbox{\scriptsize$\circ$}\enskip}\,,\,\,0\leq t\leq T\,, (6.2)
ηh​(0)=P​η0,\displaystyle\eta_{h}(0)=P\eta_{0}\,,

where PP is the L2L^{2}-projection operator onto Sh2​∘ S_{h}^{2}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\raise 7.3194pt\hbox{\scriptsize$\circ$}\enskip}. Obviously, (6.2)(\ref{eq62}) has a unique solution that satisfies e.g. ‖ηh​(t)‖≤‖ηh​(0)‖\|\eta_{h}(t)\|\leq\|\eta_{h}(0)\|, t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Recall that we have ‖v−P​v‖≤C​h2​‖v‖2\|v-Pv\|\leq Ch^{2}\|v\|_{2} for v∈H2v\in H^{2} with v⁡(0)=0v(0)=0, and ‖v−P​v‖∞≤C​h2​‖v‖2,∞\|v-Pv\|_{\infty}\leq Ch^{2}\|v\|_{2,\infty} for v∈C2v\in C^{2} with v⁡(0)=0v(0)=0. To do this, we first prove a lemma along the lines of the proof of Lemma 5.65.6.

(The temporal discretization was effected with the Crank-Nicolson implicit scheme with time step k=h/3k=h/3 in all cases; this time step was sufficiently small to ensure that the temporal error was about two orders of magnitude less than the spatial error in all cases.) The L2L^{2} errors and associated rates of convergence of the numerical scheme at t=T=0.5t=T=0.5 for diminishing h=1/Nh=1/N are shown in Table 6.1. Recall that if η0​(x)=xk​exp⁡(x)\eta_{0}(x)=x^{k}\exp(x), k=1,2,3,…k=1,2,3,\dots, the solution η⁡(x,t)\eta(x,t) of (6.1)(\ref{eq61}) is in Ck−1​(0,1)C^{k-1}(0,1) (and piecewise C∞C^{\infty}) for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. The L2L^{2} orders of convergence turn out to be practically equal to 22 for k=4k=4 and k=3k=3 in agreement with the error estimate that was proved. The rate is apparently converging to one in the case k=1k=1 in which (6.1)(\ref{eq61}) possesses a generalized, piecewise smooth solution, while in the borderline case k=2k=2 the convergence rate has not stabilized. (When we increased the number of spatial intervals NN, we observed that this rate fell steadily and was e.g. equal to 1.98261.9826 at N=1600N=1600.)

6.2. A hyperbolic equation with a variable coefficient that vanishes at the boundary

Consider the problem

ηt+(uη)x=0,0≤x≤1,    0≤t≤T,\displaystyle\eta_{t}+(u\eta)_{x}=0\,,\quad 0\leq x\leq 1\,,\,\,\,\,0\leq t\leq T\,, (6.12)
η(x,0)=η0(x),0≤x≤1,\displaystyle\eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\,,\quad 0\leq x\leq 1\,,

where uu is a given smooth function that vanishes at x=0x=0 and at x=1x=1. No boundary conditions are imposed on η\eta. The problem is well posed and may be solved by the method of characteristics. Uniqueness of solutions follows easily: If we multiply the p.d.e. in (6.12)(\ref{eq612}) by η\eta and integrate over [0,1][0,1] by parts we see that for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T

12​dd​t​‖η‖2+12​∫01η2​ux​𝑑x=0,\tfrac{1}{2}\tfrac{d}{dt}\|\eta\|^{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\eta^{2}u_{x}dx=0\,,

from which, by Gronwall’s Lemma, there follows that

‖η⁡(t)‖≤C​‖η0‖,0≤t≤T,\|\eta(t)\|\leq C\|\eta_{0}\|\,,\quad 0\leq t\leq T\,,

where C=C⁡(T,max0≤t≤T⁡‖ux‖∞)C=C(T,\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\|u_{x}\|_{\infty}).

An optimal-order L2L^{2} error estimate for the standard Galerkin semidiscretization in Sh2S_{h}^{2} on a uniform mesh may be proved for this problem using the methods previously developed in this paper. (This was first pointed out in [3].) The semidiscrete problem consists in finding ηh:[0,T]→Sh2\eta_{h}:[0,T]\to S_{h}^{2} so that

(ηh​t,ϕ)+((uηh)x,ϕ)=0,∀ϕ∈Sh2,    0≤t≤T,\displaystyle(\eta_{ht},\phi)+((u\eta_{h})_{x},\phi)=0\,,\quad\forall\phi\in S_{h}^{2}\,,\,\,\,\,0\leq t\leq T\,, (6.13)
ηh​(0)=P​η0,\displaystyle\eta_{h}(0)=P\eta_{0}\,,

where PP is the L2L^{2} projection onto Sh2S_{h}^{2}.

Suppose that u∈C02u\in C_{0}^{2} and that the solution of (6.12)(\ref{eq612}) satisfies η∈C⁡(0,T,C4)\eta\in C(0,T;C^{4}). Then

max0≤t≤T⁡‖η−ηh‖∞≤C​h2.\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\|\eta-\eta_{h}\|_{\infty}\leq Ch^{2}\,.
Proof.

Putting θ=P​η−ηh\theta=P\eta-\eta_{h}, ρ=η−P​η\rho=\eta-P\eta we have for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T that

(θt,ϕ)+((u​θ)x,ϕ)+((u​ρ)x,ϕ)=0∀ϕ∈Sh2.(\theta_{t},\phi)+((u\theta)_{x},\phi)+((u\rho)_{x},\phi)=0\quad\forall\phi\in S_{h}^{2}\,. (6.14)

we have that ‖ζ‖≤C​h3\|\zeta\|\leq Ch^{3}. Therefore, putting ϕ=θ\phi=\theta in (6.13)(\ref{eq613}) and using integration by parts we see that

‖θ‖≤C​h3.\|\theta\|\leq Ch^{3}\,.

This observation may prove useful in the error analysis of first-order problems with advection terms of the form (u​η)x(u\eta)_{x}, where uu satisfies Dirichlet boundary conditions. However, as we saw in Section 22 in the case of the Boussinesq systems under study the presence of the linear uxu_{x} term in the first p.d.e. of (CB)(\ref{cb}) or (SCB)(\ref{scb}) is the obstacle that prevents achieving optimal-order estimates. For example, examining the proof of Theorem 2.12.1 we note that if the uxu_{x} term was missing, then the terms (ξx,ϕ)(\xi_{x},\phi) and (σx,ϕ)(\sigma_{x},\phi) would not be present in (2.21)(\ref{eq221}) and, consequently, by appeal to Lemma 2.22.2 with w⁡(0)=w⁡(1)=0w(0)=w(1)=0, the estimates of the terms in (2.24)(\ref{eq224}) would lead to an O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) bound in the right-hand side of (2.25)(\ref{eq225}).

6.3. Numerical experiments with nonuniform meshes

When we used a quasiuniform mesh in the standard Galerkin semidiscretization (6.2)(\ref{eq62}) of the initial-boundary-value problem (6.1)(\ref{eq61}), numerical results (not shown here) indicating that the L2L^{2} error ‖η−ηh‖\|\eta-\eta_{h}\| is of O⁡(h)O(h); of the same order of accuracy is of course the upper bound of the L2L^{2} error predicted in a straightforward manner by the theory.

The same differences between the cases of uniform and nonuniform meshes apparently also persist in the case of first-order hyperbolic systems. Consider, for example, the following initial-boundary-value problem for the nonhomogeneous wave equation written in first-order system form:

ηt+ux=f,ut+ηx=g,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\eta_{t}+u_{x}=f\,,\\ &u_{t}+\eta_{x}=g\,,\end{aligned} 0≤x≤1,   0≤t≤T,\displaystyle 0\leq x\leq 1\,,\,\,\,0\leq t\leq T\,, (6.15)
η⁡(x,0)=η0​(x),\displaystyle\eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\,, u(x,0)=u0(x),     0≤x≤1,\displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\,,\,\,\,\,\,0\leq x\leq 1\,,
η⁡(0,t)=0,u⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\eta(0,t)=0\,,\quad\,\,u( 1,t)=0,0≤t≤T.\displaystyle 1,t)=0\,,\quad 0\leq t\leq T\,.

For the purposes of the numerical experiment we took as exact solution of (6.15)(\ref{eq615}) the pair of functions η⁡(x,t)=x​exp⁡(x⁡(t+1))\eta(x,t)=x\exp(x(t+1)), u⁡(x,t)=(x−1)​exp⁡(x​t)u(x,t)=(x-1)\exp(xt) with appropriate initial conditions and right-hand sides. We discretized the problem in space by the standard Galerkin method using piecewise linear continuous elements on a uniform mesh with meshlength h=1/Nh=1/N and also on a quasiuniform mesh with Δ​x=1.6/N\Delta x=1.6/N, h2​i−1=0.75​Δ​xh_{2i-1}=0.75\Delta x, h2​i=0.5​Δ​xh_{2i}=0.5\Delta x, 1≤i≤N/21\leq i\leq N/2. For the temporal discretization we used the classical, fourth-order explicit Runge-Kutta scheme with k=hk=h and k=Δ​xk=\Delta x, respectively. As initial values ηh​(0)\eta_{h}(0), uh​(0)u_{h}(0) we took the interpolants of η0\eta_{0} and u0u_{0}. The L2L^{2} errors at T=0.4T=0.4 and the corresponding orders of convergence are shown, for increasing NN, in Table 6.2(a) in the case of the quasiuniform mesh and in Table 6.2(b) for the uniform mesh. The experiment strongly suggests that the L2L^{2} errors ore of O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) for a uniform mesh and of

O⁡(Δ​x)O(\Delta x) for quasiuniform.

u(0,t)=0,u(1,t)=0,\displaystyle u(0,t)=0\,,\,\,\,\,u(1,t)=0\,, 0≤t≤T,\displaystyle 0\leq t\leq T\,,

and discretize it by the standard Galerkin method. We obtain similar results to those of Section 22 in which the dispersive term ux​x​tu_{xxt} is present instead of ux​xu_{xx}. (Cf.
